Machine Learning.title: Hierarchical Cooperative GFlowNets
Machine Learning.summary: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are trained to sample objects from compositional spaces with probability proportional to a reward function, but ineffective exploration can cause learned samplers to concentrate on a few high-reward regions. An intuitive remedy is to train multiple GFlowNets independently in parallel and combine their samples. However, this does not prevent multiple models from collapsing onto the same high-reward areas, leaving large regions of the state space unexplored. With this in mind, we propose Hierarchical Cooperative GFlowNets (HCG), an approach that dynamically partitions the search space to coordinate discovery without relying on hand-crafted boundaries. HCG imposes an ordering in which the highest-ranked model may explore the entire space, while lower-ranked models are progressively pushed toward regions not covered by higher-ranked ones. We provide a theoretical characterization of how specific learning objectives can shift probability mass away from designated areas, instantiating this mechanism within our architecture. A shared classifier coordinates the hierarchy by partitioning the search space, keeping the GFlowNets independently parameterized and enabling asynchronous training. Furthermore, we derive a normalizer-weighted aggregation rule for the ensemble and prove that it recovers the target reward-proportional distribution under the stated assumptions. Finally, experiments across multimodal distributions, sequence generation, combinatorial optimization, and biological sequence design show that HCG improves mode coverage and target approximation, translating increases in the number of coordinated samplers into broader, complementary exploration.

Machine Learning.title: VLN on the Fly: An Onboard Vision-Language Navigation Stack for Aerial Robots
Machine Learning.summary: Running vision-language navigation fully onboard an aerial robot is hard, since grounding, planning, and control must share limited compute and a single-stage error is difficult to isolate in flight. End-to-end aerial policies fuse these stages into one network, giving up the observability and safety checks a modular stack keeps available. We propose VLN on the Fly, an onboard stack that keeps grounding, planning, and control as separate, inspectable stages. A quantized VLM grounds an instruction to a coarse image cell, depth lifts it to a 3D goal, a fast B-spline planner returns a feasible trajectory, and a pretrained reinforcement learning policy tracks it to motor commands across quadrotors. Across 15 onboard flights over three everyday referents in a controlled indoor volume, the stack reaches the target in 13 of 15 trials with 5.72 cm mean goal error and 39.3% average GPU utilization. In 6 additional cluttered-environment trials, the stack tracks collision-free trajectories under onboard perception gating.

Machine Learning.title: DiVeR: Decision-Critical Verifier Learning for VLA Test-Time Scaling
Machine Learning.summary: Scaling robot data and model capacity has improved Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, but further progress is constrained by the high cost of robotic data. Verifier-guided test-time scaling offers an efficient alternative by sampling multiple action candidates and selecting the one most likely to lead to task success at inference time. Existing classification-based verifiers learn from trajectory-level outcomes but treat all visited states equally, even though their value for candidate discrimination can vary across a trajectory. At many states, plausible actions are similar and provide limited discrimination signal, while only a sparse set of decision-critical states admits meaningfully different actions that can substantially affect downstream outcomes. To address this, we propose DiVeR, which estimates decision criticality from the dispersion of sampled action representations. DiVeR then uses this signal to reweight verifier learning toward states where action selection is most consequential, without requiring step-level annotations or additional environment interaction. Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 robot, DiVeR consistently improves task success through more effective verifier-guided action selection, while adding negligible verifier inference overhead.

Machine Learning.title: Performance of Neural Operator Baselines on 'The Well' Dataset
Machine Learning.summary: The Well, a 15-terabyte dataset spanning 16 physical simulation domains, provides an extensive benchmark for developing and evaluating machine learning surrogate models for complex physical systems. The baselines released with the benchmark were presented by their authors as illustrative examples obtained at small computational cost, trained with zero to very limited hyperparameter tuning and under a highly constraining 12-hour per-run wall-clock limit. These results have subsequently been treated as fully tuned benchmarks, and in some cases effectively interpreted as unconstrained performance baselines. We perform a short non-exhaustive hyperparameter search for the Tucker-factorized Fourier Neural Operator (TFNO) under the same 12-hour per-run wall-clock limit, while using only a single input timestep rather than the history of up to four used by the published baselines. Despite this more restrictive setup, tuning alone reduces VRMSE below both published FNO and TFNO baselines on 15 of 17 tasks, sometimes by several orders of magnitude. This sensitivity to a modest tuning effort underscores that the released neural operator baselines should not be treated as architectural benchmarks.

Machine Learning.title: QECGBERT: A Scalable ECG Foundation Model Based on Self-Supervised Language Learning via VQ-VAE Waveform Tokenization
Machine Learning.summary: AI foundation models play a pivotal role in advancing heart disease diagnosis from electrocardiogram (ECG) data, particularly for rare diseases where the lack of sufficient labeled data hinders supervised learning. However, most self-supervised learning methods treat ECGs as generic sequence or image data without exploiting underlying physiological structure. To address this limitation, we propose QECGBERT, a self-supervised ECG language model that explicitly encodes physiological semantics by tokenizing the P, QRS, T, and isoelectric background waveforms. Vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) tokenization is applied to each 12-lead ECG, with tokens enriched by continuous waveform features to preserve morphology lost during quantization without increasing sequence length. This design enables compact BERT masked language modeling with short sequences, improving scalability and reducing computational cost relative to long-sequence approaches. QECGBERT applies BERT pre-training to the MIMIC-IV dataset containing over 800,000 unlabeled ECG recordings, and fine-tuning on labeled PTB-XL, CPSC2018, and Chapman--Shaoxing--Ningbo datasets for evaluation. The results demonstrate that QECGBERT achieves comparable or superior performance to published benchmarks, offering a scalable, physiologically aware approach to ECG foundation modeling for cardiac diagnosis.
Machine Learning.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027

Machine Learning.title: Minimaxity and Admissibility of Bayesian Neural Networks
Machine Learning.summary: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a natural probabilistic formulation for inference in deep learning models. Despite their popularity, their optimality has received limited attention through the lens of statistical decision theory. In this paper, we study decision rules induced by deep, fully connected feedforward ReLU BNNs in the normal location model under quadratic loss. We show that, for fixed prior scales, the induced Bayes decision rule is not minimax. We then propose a hyperprior on the effective output variance of the BNN prior that yields a superharmonic square-root marginal density, establishing that the resulting decision rule is simultaneously admissible and minimax. We further extend these results from the quadratic loss setting to the predictive density estimation problem with Kullback--Leibler loss. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings numerically through simulation.

Machine Learning.title: From Truncation to Commitment: Persistent Context in Uniform Discrete Diffusion
Machine Learning.summary: Uniform-state discrete diffusion models update all tokens in parallel while keeping every position revisable. Even when the commonly used top-$p$ rule leaves only one candidate at a position, that choice affects only the current reverse step and can be revised at the next sampling step. We ask what changes when selected hypotheses instead become persistent context for later predictions. We therefore propose committed reveal sampling (CRS), a training-free sampler that stores selected argmax tokens and inserts them into subsequent model inputs. Our analysis separates persistent context from truncation. Within one reverse step, adaptive top-$p$, randomized or not, reproduces the update induced by a visible token only when a likelihood-ratio ordering holds, while in a simple latent-mode model, keeping the selected token visible helps later parallel predictions agree on the same sequence-level choice. Empirically, paired experiments on Duo-distilled then separate this persistent effect from single-step top-$p$ restriction and scalar temperature scaling. Under the same finalization rule, CRS without top-$p$ truncation reaches lower generative perplexity (GenPPL) than fixed $p=0.95$ and $p=0.9$ baselines across budgets of 8--64 function evaluations (NFE). At 64 NFE, the comparison at matched unigram entropy also gives lower GenPPL for CRS, shifting the GenPPL--entropy tradeoff under this metric. Base Duo shows the same direction in a descriptive comparison, while other diversity and continuation metrics can rank these operating points differently. A distributional distance to held-out text (SOL) under a fixed GPT-2-Large representation also decreases with persistent context at the same late top-$p$ threshold. These results identify support restriction and persistent context as distinct controls of that tradeoff.

Machine Learning.title: How Do Small Coding Agents Use Code Graphs and Embeddings?
Machine Learning.summary: Coding agents are given embedding search and code-graph tools on the premise that a repository's structure is something the model lacks and the tool supplies. We test that premise on SWE-bench Verified with small open-weight models, stratifying tasks by a deterministic hop depth (the shortest code-graph path from code the issue mentions to code the gold patch changes) that a companion paper defines and validates. First, we ablate a localization agent's tool set (grep only; +embedding search; +graph tools; all) on a depth-balanced 160-task split and on all 500 tasks for ten models (six Qwen3 sizes from 0.6B to 32B with five decodings each, an FP8 control, three Gemma 4 sizes; 79k episodes). Structured tools double grep-only accuracy for Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 E4B; their gain peaks at 17-21 points at 1.7-4B and falls to 4-5 points at 32B (odds ratio 0.77-0.82 per doubling of parameters). From 8B up, about half of that gain is the form of the submission rather than finding the target; the fall from 14B to 32B is a fall in tool uptake at equal grep-only accuracy; and the same 4B size gains or does not gain from a tool depending on the checkpoint. Each extra hop multiplies the odds of correct localization by 0.50-0.67 at every size, and no tool set flattens that gradient: traces show the graph tools' gain is name lookup at hop 0 and one expansion at hop 1, and agents chain expansions in only 12-14% of episodes. A fixed repair model resolves 6-13 of 160 tasks from these localizations (oracle 26). Second, linear probes find direct call edges decodable under a within-anchor, degree-stratified protocol (AUC 0.74; 0.61-0.66 inside agent conversations), but below a lexical baseline (0.99), with two-hop edges at 0.57. Small agents carry a one-hop, largely lexical picture of their repository, in weights and in use. We release the agent, probes, logs and traces.
Machine Learning.comment: 29 pages, 5 figures. Depth labels and dataset card and full code, raw results and analysis will be released in the near future

Machine Learning.title: A Nonconvex Framework for Joint Sparse Sample Weighting and Parameter Estimation
Machine Learning.summary: We propose a joint sparse sample weighting and parameter estimation (SWAPE) framework that jointly optimizes model parameters and sample weights to train a model while simultaneously assigning an individual weight to each training data point. Our framework accommodates several widely used loss functions for the model parameters, including convex, weakly convex, and difference-of-convex loss, and weakly convex sparsity functions to control the complexity of the sample weights. To solve the resulting bivariate problem, we propose an alternating minimization method in which the subproblems for updating the model parameters and weights are each approximated using majorize-minimize techniques. We provide several approximation methods for the loss functions considered in this paper, and show the overall algorithm's convergence. Numerical experiments on various learning tasks and data anomaly settings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in minimizing the impact of undesirable data points compared to benchmark methods.

Machine Learning.title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
Machine Learning.summary: Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improvement through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale benchmark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows. CLE comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. Across 17 harness-model configurations using frontier LLMs, feedback and revision yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points. Yet the best-performing system clears only 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels in just 23.3% of tasks, highlighting the difficulty of sustained learning from experience for existing frontier LLMs. As such, the dataset can also be used to post-train LLMs to strengthen their continual learning capabilities.

Machine Learning.title: Data-driven Discovery of Lie Symmetries and First Integrals with Latent ODEs
Machine Learning.summary: We present LatentLieODE, a novel neural ODE method to discover linear Lie symmetries and first integrals of the learned dynamics from timeseries observations such as video inputs. It starts with an autoencoder, which learns a low dimensional representation of the observed system and then maps trajectories to decorrelated latent coordinates $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$. A bank of linear infinitesimal generators $\mathbf{A}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ is fitted jointly against a differentiable Lie-bracket residual $\mathbf{J}_f(z)\mathbf{A}z - \mathbf{A} f(z)$, while an MLP optimises the latent ODE $f(z) = \mathrm{d}z/\mathrm{d}t$ to reconstruct the observation-space timeseries. After suitable generators and $f$ are found, we fit a third network $H_φ$ to generate the first integral of the system. Across six benchmark systems (harmonic oscillator, simple and twin pendulums, Lotka-Volterra, pixel pendulum, sphere geodesics) we find each system's relevant symmetries, and the discovered invariants match ground-truth conserved quantities at $|ρ| \geq 0.978$. On the sphere, the pipeline recovers a non-abelian $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, certified by the negative-definite Killing form of its recovered structure constants. This work presents significant advances in data-driven discovery of symmetries and provides a new pathway for neural surrogates of dynamical systems.

Machine Learning.title: Generalization in Learning: Eyring Formula and Predator-prey Model
Machine Learning.summary: In this work, generalization in machine learning is investigated using a predator-prey model. We overview biological and chemical interpretation of the stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics and generative adversarial network. For a particular example of recovering an unknown function by a polynomial of fixed degree from a set of noisy data, the predator-prey model provides better approximation compared to the gradient descent method. Further, thermodynamical arguments, in particular Eyring formula, are used to explain grokking (delayed generalization) phenomenon in machine learning.

Machine Learning.title: Condition-Enhanced Generative Adversarial Network for Aerodynamic Configuration Design of Commercial Aircraft
Machine Learning.summary: Generative machine learning provides an end-to-end framework for aerodynamic design optimization by generating diverse aerodynamic configurations conditioned on target performance. However, the generated designs may violate geometric constraints or deviate from the prescribed aerodynamic performance. Therefore, we propose a Condition-Enhanced Generative Adversarial Network (CEGAN) that embeds geometric and aerodynamic information into the generative process. A condition-informed loss function is developed by combining a geometry-guided feasibility penalty with an aerodynamic performance penalty evaluated by surrogate models trained on the same dataset. Additionally, an output filtering mechanism discards infeasible designs using these surrogate models, ensuring compliance with prescribed conditions. The method is demonstrated on aircraft configurations similar to the Cessna Citation X. Each configuration is represented by 28 shape parameters, whose aerodynamic performance is evaluated using OpenVSP. Interpolation and extrapolation tests are conducted for different network architectures and conditioning strategies. Compared with the baseline model, CEGAN reduces the average generation error by at least 36% for interpolated conditions and by at least 46% under extreme extrapolation conditions, while successfully producing diverse and physically feasible designs that extend beyond the training distribution. Therefore, the proposed CEGAN framework offers a robust and accurate tool for rapid aerodynamic configuration exploration during the conceptual design phase.

Machine Learning.title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving
Machine Learning.summary: While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute. We study this question with h1, a simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without imposing a decomposition or search structure. h1 reaches state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to solve open problems. Through ablations and matched-model comparisons with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve rate. We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk of bitter lessons.

Machine Learning.title: Knowledge distillation across teacher architectures for compact diabetic retinopathy grading
Machine Learning.summary: Diabetic retinopathy grading from retinal fundus photographs is important but difficult to deploy on resource-constrained hardware. We conducted a controlled study of offline response-based knowledge distillation for five-class diabetic retinopathy grading on APTOS 2019, comparing ResNet-50, MobileNetV3-Large, and Swin Transformer-Tiny (Swin-T) teachers distilled into a MobileNetV3-Small student. A 3 x 4 x 2 grid of teacher, temperature, and hard-label weight was screened at one seed, while six configurations and the no-distillation baseline were evaluated across three seeds. The highest observed single-seed quadratic weighted kappa was 0.9093 (macro-F1 0.6851) for Swin-T at temperature 4 and hard-label weight 0.7; the corresponding three-seed mean was 0.9024, compared with 0.8804 for the baseline. The student used 1.52 M parameters and 5.94 MB, representing an 18.07x parameter reduction relative to Swin-T. Temperature and hard-label weight effects were teacher- and configuration-dependent, while small performance differences were sensitive to random seed. Knowledge distillation produced a compact student with competitive performance under the evaluated protocol, but independent external validation remains necessary.
Machine Learning.comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 18 tables. Submitted to PLOS ONE

Machine Learning.title: From Slices to Volumes: Comparing 2D, 2.5D, and 3D Residual Networks for Pulmonary Nodule Malignancy-Risk Classification
Machine Learning.summary:
Purpose: To compare 2D, 2.5D, and 3D residual networks for pulmonary nodule malignancy-risk classification and evaluate momentum-contrast pretraining, mild augmentation, and exclusion of indeterminate ratings.
  Methods: A retrospectively prepared LIDC-IDRI cohort contained 2,654 nodules labeled benign, indeterminate, or malignant using median radiologist ratings. Patient-disjoint splits comprised 1,876 training, 382 validation, and 396 test nodules. Representations included one axial slice, five neighboring slices, and a local CT volume. Each track evaluated a randomly initialized baseline, momentum-contrast pretraining followed by fine-tuning, and supervised training with mild augmentation. Checkpoints were selected by validation Macro-F1. The 2D experiments used three seeds; 2.5D and 3D results were single-run estimates. A separate binary experiment excluded indeterminate nodules.
  Results: Augmented models achieved test Macro-F1 values of $0.6134\pm0.0075$ for 2D, $0.6537$ for 2.5D, and $0.5403$ for 3D; the 2D uncertainty denotes population standard deviation across seeds. Corresponding accuracies were $0.6128$, $0.6869$, and $0.5455$. Augmentation improved Macro-F1 within every track, whereas the tested pretraining recipes reduced it. Binary Macro-F1 values were $0.8227$, $0.8664$, and $0.7554$, respectively.
  Conclusion: Augmented 2.5D achieved the highest observed performance. Differences in preprocessing, optimization, capacity, and replication limit attribution to dimensionality. Labels reflect radiologist-assessed malignancy risk rather than pathology-confirmed cancer. Code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/CT-DeepLearning-Team/CT-2D-2.5D-3D-DeepLearning.

Machine Learning.title: Exponential Wake-Up Overshoot in Explicit Gaussian Point-Process Filters
Machine Learning.summary: When events resume after a long silence, explicit Gaussian point-process filters amplify the first update exponentially in the silence duration. We give the exact distribution of this update and a computable index that predicts when it overshoots. For the explicit (single-scoring-step) filter and its implicit posterior-mode counterpart, we derive second-order silence expansions of the state variance with opposite-sign logarithmic corrections. The crossing index determines when the post-wake prediction exceeds the resumed rate, separating the bin width at which the amplification exponent reaches one from the larger width at which the true rate is overshot. At fixed bin width, the implicit filter's expected loss grows logarithmically with silence duration, whereas a continuous-time counterexample rules out a bound uniform in bin width and silence duration. Experimental evaluation confirms these predictions in all 73 crossing cells and on exchange trade data, while variance caps reduce explicit overshoot but mostly hurt the implicit filter.
Machine Learning.comment: 26 pages, 3 figures, 13 tables; main text with Appendices A-G (proofs, experimental protocol, additional results). A four-page version has been submitted to IEEE Signal Processing Letters

Machine Learning.title: Distributed LLM Inference via Communication-Efficient Speculative Decoding
Machine Learning.summary: Distributed speculative decoding has emerged as a promising approach for device--server collaborative large language model (LLM) inference, but its decoding speedup is often limited by the vocabulary-scale communication overhead. In existing distributed speculative decoding methods, exact rejection sampling requires transmitting full token distributions over the LLM vocabulary between the device and the server, which becomes costly in bandwidth-constrained environments. To address this issue, we propose DISCO, a communication-efficient framework for distributed speculative decoding, that eliminates vocabulary-scale distribution transfer while preserving the exact target distribution. DISCO achieves this by introducing a server-side replica of the draft small language model (SLM), which enables the server to locally obtain the draft-side distribution required for rejection sampling. As a result, DISCO exchanges only drafted token indices and scalar probability values between the device and the server. Experimental results on multiple datasets show that DISCO consistently achieves higher decoding speedup than existing distributed speculative decoding methods, particularly under stringent bandwidth constraints.

Machine Learning.title: ResCom: Activation Residual Compensation for Large Language Model Quantization
Machine Learning.summary: Low-bit weight--activation quantization reduces the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models, but activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration. Reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot distinguish activations within the same quantization bin. We propose ResCom, a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error. An output-aware calibration procedure selects residual directions by their contribution to output reconstruction and computes the correction in closed form, without gradient training or updates to the calibrated weights. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, improve MMLU by 2.89 percentage points, and raise five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96 to 36.16 percent. Evaluations on models from 1B to 70B parameters and on held-out C4 test the method beyond this setting. The evaluated FP32 implementation adds 2.25 percent to 4K prefill time; a separate compact-storage implementation retains a 27.7 percent peak-memory reduction relative to FP16.
Machine Learning.comment: 25 pages (10 pages main text + appendix), 9 figures, 20 tables

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Linear-Core Surrogates: Smooth Loss Functions with Linear Rates for Classification and Structured Prediction
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: A fundamental dichotomy in the theory of classification sets smoothness against statistical efficiency: smooth surrogate losses such as the logistic loss enable fast $O(1/T)$ optimization but yield slow square-root $H$-consistency bounds, while piecewise-linear losses like the Hinge loss achieve optimal linear $H$-consistency rates but are non-differentiable. We introduce Linear-Core (LC) Surrogates, the first family of explicit convex loss functions that provably resolve this tension. By stitching a linear core to a smooth tail, we construct surrogates that are differentiable everywhere ($C^1$, and even $C^2$ under mild conditions) while retaining strict linear $H$-consistency bounds, the strongest known form of consistency guarantee. We establish these linear bounds across three increasingly complex settings: binary classification, multi-class classification, and structured prediction. To our knowledge, this is the first explicit construction to simultaneously achieve smoothness and linear $H$-consistency in any of these settings. Beyond their theoretical appeal, Linear-Core Surrogates offer practical advantages. In multi-class classification, their constant gradient profile near the decision boundary provides natural robustness to instance-dependent label noise, outperforming Cross-Entropy by 2.6% on corrupted CIFAR-10. In structured prediction, their smoothness enables an unbiased stochastic gradient estimator that bypasses the $O(|Y|^2)$ per-step complexity of exact inference, yielding a 23$\times$ speedup over Structured SVMs on large-vocabulary sequence tagging tasks.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Valid Early Detection of Memorization in Diffusion Models
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion models can sometimes reproduce examples from their training data, a phenomenon known as memorization. Existing memorization detection methods for unconditional diffusion models typically operate at a pre-selected timestep and therefore cannot adapt the detection time to the evolving denoising trajectory. Sequential monitoring enables adaptive detection but repeated testing across timesteps complicates trajectory-level false-alarm control. We study two ways of combining split conformal calibration with sequential monitoring for prompt-free memorization detection: per-step Bonferroni calibration and direct trajectory-level calibration of the maximum memorization score. The former controls repeated testing by splitting the false-alarm budget across timesteps, whereas the latter calibrates the event of ever crossing a threshold directly through the trajectory-level maximum. We evaluate this formulation on an unconditional CIFAR-10 EDM using two complementary per-step statistics based on geometry and representation spikiness. Experiments show that sequential monitoring improves the power-timing tradeoff over fixed-time detection. Compared with Bonferroni calibration, trajectory-level calibration achieves comparable detection power while using the false-alarm budget less conservatively and enabling earlier detection at higher noise levels.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: Extended version of a 4-page paper accepted as a poster at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on E-Values: From Statistics to ML. 13 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables

Statistical Machine Learning.title: The Tamed Subgradient Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm beyond Convexity
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study the problem of sampling from target distributions whose potentials are simultaneously non-smooth, subject to superlinear gradient growth, and non-convex. We introduce the Subgradient Tamed Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (SG-TULA), a discretisation of the Langevin diffusion that operates directly on subgradients, without relying on computationally demanding smoothing procedures. To handle the superlinear regime, taming techniques are employed to produce a stable, explicit scheme. We derive non-asymptotic convergence bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance, with all constants tracked explicitly in terms of dimension and inverse temperature, improving upon the currently known rates for subgradient-based Langevin algorithms. We further provide excess risk estimates for the associated optimisation problem. We verify the assumptions, with explicit constants, for the regularized pretraining potential of a LLM in the GPT-2 lineage and the boosted coordinate-wise variant of SG-TULA pretrains the former competitively against finetuned AdamW and Muon, for which no comparable non-asymptotic guarantees are presently available.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: How Much Graph Is Too Much? Graph Construction and Exposure in Spatio-Temporal Forecasting
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Spatio-temporal graph neural networks combine a node's history with information from graph neighbors. The central question is whether graph neighbors provide predictive information beyond each node's own history. Forecast accuracy depends on both the choice of neighbors and the way graph messages enter the temporal model. We study these choices as graph construction and graph exposure on U.S. state unemployment, traffic speed, and electricity demand. Our diagnostic design uses two comparisons: varying exposure while holding the domain graph fixed, and varying construction while holding late gated integration fixed. A GRU using only each node's own history and randomized graph controls help assess what the graph contributes. Under a common change forecasting protocol, the same domain graph can improve or worsen error relative to the GRU across integration designs. Late integration alone is insufficient, while adding a fusion gate yields lower mean error in all three tasks. With late gated integration fixed, a graph based on residual correlations has the lowest mean error among the tested graphs, although randomized graphs perform similarly on unemployment. The findings support evaluating graph construction and integration together, with conclusions tied to the comparisons actually performed.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Ask to Learn: Query-Based Collaborative Reinforcement Learning
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Offline reinforcement learning is fundamentally limited by the coverage of the available data, while collecting additional trajectories through online exploration may be costly, unsafe, or infeasible. We study whether this limitation can be overcome without directly interacting with the underlying environment. Motivated by practical settings such as collaborator-mediated simulation, where a collaborator can provide information complementary to the offline data, we introduce query-based collaborative reinforcement learning to study how to acquire this information efficiently. The learner starts with a fixed offline dataset and adaptively queries state-time pairs; the collaborator samples an action according to a fixed, possibly suboptimal policy, and the simulator returns the corresponding reward and next state. For finite-horizon tabular problems, we derive an instance-dependent information-theoretic lower bound on the additional queries required to identify an $ε$-optimal policy and develop a local quadratic approximation. Guided by this characterization, we develop an adaptive query-allocation algorithm whose query complexity nearly matches the local benchmark under suitable conditions. Experiments on multiple synthetic and semi-synthetic environments demonstrate the empirical efficiency of the proposed method.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: HIFI: A Highly Efficient Framework for Statistical Inference with Foundation Models
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Foundation models provide powerful representations for unstructured data, such as text and images, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) makes their adaptation to downstream tasks increasingly practical. For neural estimators that lack a tractable sampling distribution, resampling-based procedures offer a flexible route to statistical inference, but they often require hundreds of model fits, making them computationally prohibitive at foundation-model scale. We introduce HIFI, a two-stage fine-tuning framework for statistical inference on parameters such as conditional means. Stage 1 adapts a foundation model once on a larger sample, capturing the complex structure of the data and controlling estimation bias through a single fit. Stage 2 applies a resampling inference procedure to a smaller independent sample, concurrently fitting multiple lightweight PEFT estimators to the residual to quantify estimation variability without relearning the full task. HIFI accommodates a broad class of resampling procedures, including ensemble subsampling and the nonparametric bootstrap. Across vision and text experiments, HIFI scales to pretrained models ranging from tens of millions to more than ten billion parameters while providing accurate point estimates and well-calibrated confidence intervals across diverse architectures, and reduces training compute by up to 91.9% relative to direct resampling. An application to gene-expression inference illustrates the practical value of the framework for uncertainty-aware scientific inference.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Joint Independence Testing for Latent Position Random Graphs
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Kernel techniques are among the most powerful methods in data science and statistics. One of the key properties of kernels contributing to their numerous successful applications is that the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space is expressive enough to encode probability distributions without loss of information or to capture the joint independence of $M\ge 2$ random variables, under mild conditions. Computationally, these measures (i) rely on the so-called Gram matrix which contains the pairwise similarity of sample points, and (ii) converge at a rate $O \left(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)$, where $n$ denotes the sample size. We focus on measuring the independence of latent position random graphs (LPRGs), a model widely-applied for instance in neuroscience, sociology, and epidemiology. In LPRGs a latent representation is associated to each node. The similarity of these representations (meant via a kernel) determines whether two nodes are connected, making the Gram matrices only implicitly observable and the estimation challenging. Despite the fundamental importance of quantifying the independence of $M$ LPRGs, very little is known about the solution of this problem; existing techniques are restricted to $M=2$ components and only guarantee consistency without rates. In this work, (i) we define an independence measure called graph Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (GHSIC) for $M\ge 2$ LPRGs, (ii) we prove that it can be estimated at a rate $\tilde{O}\left(n^{-\frac{1}{3}}\right)$ relying on spectral decomposition of adjacency matrices, (iii) without the need to choose kernels and their hyperparameters. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed GHSIC estimator both on synthetic examples and in the analysis of brain functional connectivity subnetworks in natural language perception.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Simultaneous analysis of approximate leave-one-out cross-validation and mean-field inference
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Approximate Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (ALO-CV) is a method that has been proposed to estimate the generalization error of a regularized estimator in the high-dimensional regime where dimension and sample size are of the same order, the so-called ``proportional regime''. A new analysis is developed to derive the consistency of ALO-CV for non-differentiable regularizers under Gaussian covariates and strong convexity. Using a conditioning argument, the difference between the ALO-CV weights and their counterparts in mean-field inference is shown to be small. Combined with upper bounds between the mean-field inference estimate and the leave-one-out quantity, this provides a proof that ALO-CV approximates the leave-one-out quantity up to negligible error terms. Linear models with square loss, robust linear regression and single-index models are explicitly treated.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Graph Neural Networks for Supply Chain Management: A Framework and Real World Benchmark
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently gained traction in transportation, bioinformatics, language and image processing, but research on their application to supply chain management remains limited. Supply chains are inherently graph-like, making them ideal for GNN methodologies, which can optimize and solve complex problems. The barriers include a lack of proper conceptual foundations, familiarity with graph applications in SCM, and real-world benchmark datasets for GNN-based supply chain research. To address this, we discuss and connect supply chains with graph structures for effective GNN application, providing detailed formulations, examples, mathematical definitions, and task guidelines. Additionally, we present a multi-perspective real-world benchmark dataset from a leading FMCG company in Bangladesh, focusing on supply chain planning. We discuss various supply chain tasks using GNNs and benchmark several state-of-the-art models on homogeneous and heterogeneous graphs across six supply chain analytics tasks. Our analysis shows that GNN-based models consistently outperform statistical Machine Learning and other Deep Learning models by around 10-30% in regression, 10-30% in classification and detection tasks, and 15-40% in anomaly detection tasks on designated metrics. With this work, we lay the groundwork for solving supply chain problems using GNNs, supported by conceptual discussions, methodological insights, and a comprehensive dataset.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: 27 Pages. arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2401.15299

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Ambiguous Fits: The Rashomon Effect and Challenges in Scaling Law Estimation
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Estimating neural scaling laws involves an end-to-end pipeline: designing a scaling recipe, training models across scales, evaluating models on a target metric, and deploying an algorithm to fit a scaling law to the resulting data. This final fitting stage is often treated as routine: standard procedures minimize a non-convex fitting loss using local optimization from a grid of initializations, and return the best solution found. Yet such heuristic searches can fail in two distinct ways: they offer no guarantee of returning a nearly optimal solution, and they obscure whether fundamentally different parameter choices fit the data nearly as well. Indeed, we show that standard scaling law fitting is subject to a Rashomon effect (Breiman, 2001): the sublevel sets of near-minimizers correspond to broad parameter regions whose extrapolations diverge substantially at scale. We resolve these issues with a deterministic branch-and-bound algorithm that guarantees nearly optimal fitting loss and exhaustively maps the near-minimizers to the implied range of scaling curves.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: The Price of Scale in Proactive Memory Recall
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: A long-lived assistant that brings up memories without being asked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption. We show that this decision is a multiple-testing problem whose difficulty grows with the store size $N$. On streaming replays of LongMemEval and LoCoMo, a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at $N=8$ reaches 87-100% at $N=2048$, across embedding models and for explicit and implicit cues; LLM judges show the same growth from a lower base. We prove that a gate with false-alarm rate $α$ operates at a per-item false-positive rate of about $-\ln(1-α)/N$, which pins its hit rate to the far left of the single-comparison ROC curve and, under regular variation, makes it decay as a power of $N$ with an explicit constant. The resulting prediction matches the hit rate of a per-$N$ oracle threshold to within one percentage point. The analysis explains why lexical and semantic channels need thresholds growing like $\ln N$ and $\sqrt{\ln N}$, and why per-cue normalisation roughly doubles the hit rate at matched false alarms. A cue-swap conformal gate, which compares the current cue with the user's other cues on the same store, needs no labels and has a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability; on LongMemEval it holds false alarms near 5% at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold. Three annotators (Fleiss' $κ=0.63$) find that about nine in ten false alarms are genuine interruptions. Code and data: https://github.com/RiverChenStillCompiling/price-of-scale
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/RiverChenStillCompiling/price-of-scale

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Certifying Distributionally Robust Decisions from Projection Observations
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: A scalar measurement can determine a robust decision without identifying the latent covariance or every decision risk. We study finite Gaussian projection experiments with a fixed mean-plus-standard-deviation target. The observation laws define a set of indistinguishable moment models. We exhibit decisions that agree throughout that set despite unidentified risk values, and give a confidence-set certificate that returns a decision or an unresolved outcome. We prove soundness, necessary abstention for indistinguishable models with incompatible optima, and a fixed-checkpoint certification guarantee. A scalar profile reduces nonlinear risk comparisons to convex inner problems. Across seven synthetic instances, jointly calibrated moment regions give sufficient budgets 21 to 52 times explicit expected-sample information lower bounds. Separately measured stopping times are lower, with zero decision errors in 1,900 simulated streams. These comparisons do not constitute matching bounds, and the guarantees require Gaussian replication.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Intrinsic Gradient Barriers in Pushforward Deep Generative Models
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Broad classes of deep generative models (DGMs) operate by learning to map a simple source distribution, such as a standard Gaussian, to a complex high-dimensional target distribution. Despite their success, DGMs often empirically struggle to accurately represent distributions with heavy tails or well-separated modes. In this work, we show that these difficulties reflect intrinsic properties of the underlying transport problem rather than particular neural network architectures or training procedures. We establish quantitative lower bounds on the gradients and Jacobians of pushforward mappings that transport log-concave source distributions to such targets. For heavy-tailed target distributions, the required gradient magnitude grows as the target develops increasingly large moments. For multimodal target distributions, the low-probability regions between well-separated modes similarly force large gradients in the transport map. We discuss how such large derivatives relate to trade-offs between expressivity and numerical stability. Our results hold under substantially weaker regularity conditions than previous analyses and remain stable under perturbations of the target distribution. Finally, we show that these obstructions can be mitigated when the goal is approximation of a given density rather than generative modeling. Specifically, we propose simple classes of bijective reparametrizations that can alleviate the difficult geometric structure and reduce the gradient burden placed on the learned generative map. Numerical experiments support our theoretical analysis.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Indirect and noisy observations are difficult to invert when the forward operator smooths out the unknown signal. In this case, the unstable modes are precisely the modes that the data reveals least, thus the success of any reconstruction method depends on how prior information interacts with the geometry of the operator across regularity scales. Diffusion priors have become ubiquitous for such problems; however, the current theory still does not determine when a learned score remains informative under ill-posed forward operators. In this paper, we study posterior diffusion for linear inverse problems on Hilbert scales and derive a stability theory under an explicit score-amplification condition. Under a smoothing condition on the forward map, a source condition on the truth, and weak-norm control of score error, we derive non-asymptotic recovery bounds in \(\Hs^s\) that separate observation noise, score approximation, and reverse-time discretization. These bounds give a recoverable regularity threshold determined jointly by operator smoothing, truth regularity, score regularity, and the posterior correction. The threshold specifies the Hilbert-scale norms \(\Hs^s\) in which weak-norm score error remains controlled after propagation through the posterior reverse dynamics. For larger regularity indices \(s\), the inverse geometry magnifies the same error, and the Hilbert-scale recovery estimate no longer gives uniform stability. We also prove that a posterior correction adapted to the forward operator improves stability relative to isotropic guidance in the regularity ranges where the smoothing action of the forward map matters most. The recovery estimates give a regularity-sensitive theory of posterior diffusion and show how learned score error, operator smoothing, and reconstruction norm jointly determine the stable range predicted by the analysis.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Winner's Curse Drives False Promises in Data-Driven Decisions
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: A major challenge in data-driven decision-making is accurate policy evaluation---i.e., guaranteeing that a learned decision-making policy achieves the promised benefits. A popular strategy is model-based policy evaluation, which estimates a model from data to infer counterfactual outcomes. This strategy is known to produce unwarrantedly optimistic estimates of the true benefit due to the winner's curse. We searched the recent literature on data-driven decision-making, identifying a sample of 55 papers published in Management Science in the past decade; all but two relied on this flawed methodology. Several common justifications are provided: (1) the estimated models are accurate, stable, and well-calibrated, (2) the historical data uses random treatment assignment, (3) the model family is well-specified, and (4) the evaluation methodology uses sample splitting. Unfortunately, we show that no combination of these justifications avoids the winner's curse. First, we provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that the winner's curse can cause large, spurious reported benefits even when all these justifications hold. Second, we perform a simulation study based on the recent and consequential data-driven refugee matching problem. We construct a synthetic refugee matching environment (calibrated to closely match the real setting) but designed so that no assignment policy can improve expected employment compared to random assignment. Model-based methods report large, stable gains of around 60% even when the true effect is zero; these gains are on par with improvements of 22-75% reported in the literature. Our results provide strong evidence against model-based evaluation.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Inference for Causal Path-Specific Effects in Longitudinal Studies with Repeated Treatments and Multiple Mediators
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: In longitudinal studies, repeated treatments may be followed by different sequences of mediators and time-varying covariates. We develop semiparametric inference for path-specific effects in this setting, allowing the number, type, and ordering of intermediate variables to vary across treatment occasions. Under consistency, positivity, edge consistency, and the cross-world restrictions of a nonparametric structural equation model with independent errors, path-specific means are identified by the edge g-formula. We derive two parameterizations of the efficient influence function of the identifying functional. The first follows the observed-data factorization and uses conditional intermediate-variable densities. The second uses sequential regressions to replace the corresponding integrations and Bayes' rule to express density ratios through treatment-history regressions, thereby avoiding direct estimation of intermediate-variable densities. Each yields a one-step estimator that permits flexible nuisance estimation. We establish product-rate conditions for asymptotic linearity and semiparametric efficiency. The density-based estimator has blockwise multiple robustness, generalizing triply robust estimation, while the regression-based estimator has sequential multiple robustness. We further develop a sensitivity analysis for selected violations of cross-world independence assumptions used to identify these effects. Simulations examine finite-sample performance and robustness to model misspecifications. An application to the Framingham Heart Study examines sustained-smoking effects on systolic blood pressure along pathways through repeated body mass index measurements. The proposed methods are implemented in the R package flexPaths on Gihub at xxou/flexPaths.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Step Lookahead Information Via Adaptive Batching
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study tabular finite-horizon reinforcement learning problems with multiple steps of lookahead information. Before acting, the learner observes $\ell$ steps of future transition and reward realizations: the exact state the agent would reach and the rewards it would collect under any possible course of action. While it has been shown that such information can drastically boost the value, finding the optimal policy is NP-hard, and it is common to apply one of two tractable heuristics: processing the lookahead in chunks of predefined sizes ('fixed batching policies'), and model predictive control. We first illustrate the problems with these two approaches and propose utilizing the lookahead in adaptive (state-dependent) batches; we refer to such policies as adaptive batching policies (ABPs). We derive the optimal Bellman equations for these strategies and design an optimistic regret-minimizing algorithm that enables learning the optimal ABP when interacting with unknown environments. Our regret bounds are order-optimal up to a potential factor of the lookahead horizon $\ell$, which can usually be considered a small constant.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Conformal Prediction with Stable Measurement Mechanisms
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: In applications such as air-quality monitoring, inexpensive sensor readings can help predict pollutant concentrations measured by a separate reference instrument. We study how to adapt conformal prediction intervals to a new population when reference outcomes are available in the source data, but only sensor readings and context, such as weather conditions, are available in the target. We assume that the measurement distribution at a given outcome and context remains stable, while context frequencies and outcome distributions may change. This model is a particular form of causal mechanism shift. Its statistical restriction has been studied as sparse joint shift. Using established marginal matching, predictive adjustment, and weighted conformal calibration, we examine what this restriction contributes to coverage and interval length for continuous outcomes. Gaussian analyses show how measurement stability can identify outcome changes and how retaining context can shorten prediction intervals. For Gaussian models with known source mechanisms, we derive exact coverage formulas in the large-calibration limit while keeping the unlabeled target sample finite. These formulas explain when sharing a correction across contexts is preferable to fitting separate corrections, and why estimating outcome variability is particularly sensitive to weakly informative measurements. Experiments on synthetic Gaussian data show a coverage gain over covariate weighting at the same mean length and a length reduction of about $8\%$ relative to pooled label adjustment at comparable coverage. On the Air Quality dataset, controlled shifts yield coverage gains with longer intervals, while spring-to-autumn and year-over-year transfers show substantial undercoverage.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Minimax PAC Bounds for Learning in Exogenous Contextual MDPs
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We introduce a PAC framework in which the learner can access sampling oracles both before and at decision time. Sample complexity is measured by a pair $(n,m)$, where $n$ is the learning budget spent before a query is known and $m$ is the additional sampling budget per query. We demonstrate its relevance in discounted Markov decision processes with exogenous i.i.d.\ contexts revealed before acting. Contexts may affect both rewards and transitions but remain uncontrolled by the agent. The learner can sample the unknown context distribution and the transition kernel. We study policy evaluation (PE), best-value estimation (BVE), and best-policy extraction (BPE). When rewards and transitions are known, a variance-reduced algorithm solves all three tasks with sample complexity $\bigl(\widetilde O((1-γ)^{-3}\varepsilon^{-2}),0\bigr)$, which is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. Let $\mathcal{X}$ be the controlled state space. When transitions are also unknown, we give a PE algorithm with complexity $\bigl(\widetilde O(|\mathcal X|(1-γ)^{-3}\varepsilon^{-2}), \widetilde O((1-γ)^{-2}\varepsilon^{-2})\bigr)$ and matching lower bounds at this budget pair. For BVE and BPE, we give an algorithm with a common offline budget $\widetilde O(|\mathcal X|^2|\mathcal A|(1-γ)^{-4}\varepsilon^{-2})$ and respective query costs $\widetilde O(|\mathcal A|(1-γ)^{-2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ and $\widetilde O(|\mathcal A|(1-γ)^{-3}\varepsilon^{-2})$. Importantly, all bounds are independent of the context-space cardinality.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Online Shift Detection and Conformal Adaptation for Deployed Safety Classifiers
Statistical Machine Learning.summary:
We study three failure modes of deployed safety classifiers: distribution shift, targeted evasion, and invalid scores from reasoning-model monitors. A reduced 800-cell subset of a pre-registered factorial (4 classifiers x 5 shifts x 20 seeds x 2 windows) gives 86.8% control-validated detection (alarm at or after onset, quiet paired no-shift stream; raw TPR 91.5%), mean latency 39.7 steps at w=100 and a classifier-by-shift crossover ($η^2 = 0.186$ complete-case; 0.02-0.03 under a censoring sensitivity analysis) that motivates per-classifier monitoring. Shifted corpora are mostly harmful prompts, so this detects a constructed score change, not accuracy loss. The density-ratio step of weighted conformal adaptation collapses for 3/4 classifiers in high-dimensional embeddings; PCA to 32 dimensions raises temporal-shift coverage (+33pp, +20.5pp).
  A score-disagreement canary (an un-targeted classifier compared with the primary) flags 37/49 (75.5%) of the GCG inputs DeBERTa scores as safe (Llama Guard pair; 93.9% best single canary), leaving a residual that evades both. For one fixed attack objective we describe a local stall condition (gap $= 1/(2λ)$; observed/predicted 0.86-1.00 at $λ\geq 2$, n=20; blocked rate does not replicate). Where both models judge content harmful there is no disagreement to detect (2%, 1/50). The best-value frontier LLM canary flags 83.7% (Wilson lower bound 71%) of 49 adversarial prompts with 7/1000 benign false positives.
  KS false-alarm rates inflate 5.4x under heterogeneous traffic; the two CUSUM runs there conflict. On o3, GCG-appended harmful inputs need 2.5x the token budget of simple benign inputs (T50 = 117 vs 46; length and content not separated), and at 16 tokens o3, o4-mini and gemini-2.5-pro all return 0/100 valid scores.

Adds rotating probes, PAIR, CUSUM/EWMA

Statistical Machine Learning.title: On the Hardness of Reinforcement Learning with Transition Look-Ahead
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study reinforcement learning (RL) with transition look-ahead, where the agent may observe which states would be visited upon playing any sequence of $\ell$ actions before deciding its course of action. While such predictive information can drastically improve the achievable performance, we show that using this information optimally comes at a potentially prohibitive computational cost. Specifically, we prove that optimal planning with one-step look-ahead ($\ell=1$) can be solved in polynomial time through a novel linear programming formulation. In contrast, for $\ell \geq 2$, the problem becomes NP-hard. Our results delineate a precise boundary between tractable and intractable cases for the problem of planning with transition look-ahead in reinforcement learning.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: MetaARIMA: Configuration-Level Transfer Learning for ARIMA Models
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Time Series Foundation Models have demonstrated that pretraining on diverse datasets enables effective transfer to new forecasting tasks. Classical methods like ARIMA, however, remain configured and trained independently for each series, discarding knowledge from previous experiments. Consequently, selecting and training an ARIMA configuration remains challenging and often relies on heuristic approaches based on in-sample goodnessof-fit measures. We propose MetaARIMA, a pretrained configuration policy based on metalearning that brings transfer learning to classical statistical forecasting at the configuration level rather than the model level. The policy learns from historical experiments which ARIMA configurations achieve top-quantile performance, and recommends promising candidates for new series while preserving interpretability and local estimation. At inference, it selects a diverse set of candidates via maximal marginal relevance and efficiently identifies the final configuration using successive halving. Experiments in a transfer learning setting, training on M4 and evaluating on M1, M3, and Tourism, show that MetaARIMA outperforms AutoARIMA and other classical methods while being more dataefficient. In a comparison with recent zero-shot foundation models, MetaARIMA remains competitive with Chronos2, Moirai2, and TimesFM. The experiments are publicly available at https://github.com/vcerqueira/experiments-metaarima.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: Conditionally accepted at the International Journal of Forecasting

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Synthetic Data Augmentation for Functional Data: Wasserstein Risk Bounds and Diffusion-Based Conditional Generation
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Functional data are costly to collect; samples of tens to hundreds of curves are common. Synthetic data augmentation can help, but its theory is developed for finite-dimensional data and relies on total variation, which is uninformative for functions. We study augmentation with a class-conditional functional diffusion generator and state guarantees in the Wasserstein-1 distance. For stable downstream estimators, we bound the risk of training on synthetic curves, from above and below, by the risk of training on as many real curves plus a generation penalty, and derive the best number of synthetic curves and a condition under which synthetic data outperform real data. For allocating synthetic curves under class imbalance, we bound the excess risk of training on real and synthetic curves together, without sample splitting. In applications to temperature, hyperspectral and gait curves, augmentation improved classification, function-to-scalar regression and function-to-function regression, and directing synthetic curves to the minority class gave the largest gain under class imbalance.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: AdamW has long been the dominant optimizer in language model pretraining, despite numerous claims that alternative optimizers offer 1.4 to 2x speedup. We posit that two methodological shortcomings have obscured fair comparisons and hindered practical adoption: (i) unequal hyperparameter tuning and (ii) limited or misleading evaluation setups. To address these two issues, we conduct a systematic study of ten deep learning optimizers across four model scales (0.1B-1.2B parameters) and data-to-model ratios (1-8x the Chinchilla optimum). We find that fair and informative comparisons require rigorous hyperparameter tuning and evaluations across a range of model scales and data-to-model ratios, performed at the end of training. First, optimal hyperparameters for one optimizer may be suboptimal for another, making blind hyperparameter transfer unfair. Second, the actual speedup of many proposed optimizers over well-tuned baselines is lower than claimed and decreases with model size to only 1.1x for 1.2B parameter models. Thirdly, comparing intermediate checkpoints before reaching the target training budgets can be misleading, as rankings between two optimizers can flip during training due to learning rate decay. Through our thorough investigation, we find that all the fastest optimizers such as Muon and Soap, use matrices as preconditioners -- multiplying gradients with matrices rather than entry-wise scalars. However, the speedup of matrix-based optimizers is inversely proportional to model scale, decreasing from 1.4x over AdamW for 0.1B parameter models to merely 1.1x for 1.2B parameter models.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: 108 pages, 8 figures, reproducible runs available at https://wandb.ai/marin-community/optimizer-scaling

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Minimax Regret for Sobolev Kernel-Based Reinforcement Learning
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study the minimax regret rate for episodic kernel-based reinforcement learning, where the expected reward and transition density belong to a Sobolev reproducing kernel Hilbert space, with continuous state and action spaces, and adversarial initial states. For Sobolev smoothness parameter $ν>0$, state dimension $d_S$, and action dimension $d_A$, we prove that the minimax expected regret over $T$ episodes is $\widetildeΘ(T^{\max\{e_A,e_B\}})$, where $e_A=\frac{ν+d_A}{2ν+d_A}$, $e_B=\frac{ν+d_A+3d_S/2}{2ν+d_A+2d_S}$ with the other model parameters fixed. The two exponents reflect the distinct difficulties of action selection and learning across states. We introduce Sobolev Optimal Value Iteration (SOVI), which attains this rate from observed rewards and transitions. For fixed smoothness and reference-kernel lengthscale, its regret bound has a prefactor polynomial in the state-action dimension $d=d_S+d_A$, horizon $H$, transition and reward RKHS norm bounds $u,B_r$, and kernel norm-comparison factor $Λ$, up to logarithmic factors. The algorithm separates initial action selection from continuation-value estimation and combines local polynomial approximation with the shared RKHS structure of the approximation errors. Our matching upper and lower bounds determine the optimal dependence on the number of episodes for Sobolev kernel-based reinforcement learning. Thus, we partially address the open problem in Vakili(2024) under the condition of the Sobolev kernel setup.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Prior-Data Fitted Networks for In-Context Off-Policy Evaluation
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) is essential for assessing decision policies before deployment when online experimentation is costly or unsafe. Accurate estimation remains difficult when behavior-policy data are limited and the target policy favors states and actions rarely observed in those data. We propose InCOPE, a prior-data fitted network that learns a shared policy-value prediction rule across synthetic OPE tasks. We construct an OPE task prior over Markov decision processes and behavior-target policy pairs, generating behavior-policy datasets and exact target-policy values for pretraining. For a new tabular decision problem, the pretrained network uses the behavior-policy dataset, target policy, and known task settings as context to predict the policy's expected return without task-specific parameter updates. Experiments across four tabular domains, including a semi-synthetic clinical setting, demonstrate InCOPE's effectiveness for policy-value estimation.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Budgeted Prompt-Set Expansion and Refinement for Language Models via Simulation Optimization
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: A prompt is an instruction or description provided by the user to guide a generative language model toward outputs that meet application requirements. When these requirements change, existing prompts may need to be adapted and improved. Evaluating candidate prompts requires time and computational resources. We therefore study how to expand and refine an initial set of prompts under a limited evaluation budget through simulation optimization, aiming to maximize a pre-defined task score for a fixed language model. Specifically, we propose a two-stage framework. In the first stage, we expand the initial set of prompts into a finite candidate set, where each prompt is represented by a moderate-dimensional vector. In the subsequent stage of evaluation and selection, we construct a surrogate model of the score for moderate-dimensional vectors representing the prompts. We propose sequentially selecting prompts for evaluation using the constructed surrogate model. We prove the consistency of the sequential evaluation procedure in our framework. We further introduce a refinement procedure that uses the collected scores to search beyond the initial candidate set. We also conduct numerical experiments to demonstrate the advantages of our method over baseline prompt selection methods, with higher prompt scores, especially when the budget for calling language models to evaluate prompts is limited.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Causal Inference Under Unmeasured Confounding With Negative Controls: A Minimax Learning Approach
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study the estimation of causal parameters when not all confounders are observed and instead negative controls are available. Recent work has shown how these can enable identification and efficient estimation via two so-called bridge functions. In this paper, we tackle the primary challenges in causal inference with negative controls: identifying and estimating these bridge functions. Previous work has typically relied on completeness conditions for identification, imposed uniqueness assumptions for estimation, and focused on parametric models for the bridge functions. Instead, we provide an alternative identification strategy that assumes the existence of two bridge functions rather than completeness conditions. We also provide new estimators for these functions based on minimax learning formulations. These estimators accommodate general function classes such as Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces and neural networks. We study finite-sample convergence results both for estimating bridge functions themselves and for the final estimation of the causal parameter under a variety of combinations of assumptions. We avoid uniqueness conditions on the bridge functions as much as possible.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: Accepted by Journal of Machine Learning Research 2026

Statistical Machine Learning.title: The Information Geometry of Representation Formation
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Most analyses of neural representations focus on trained endpoints, leaving the process by which internal structure forms comparatively unmeasured. We instead treat representation formation itself as an object of study, asking whether the path a representation takes through training reveals information that its endpoint does not. We formalize this idea by viewing representation learning as a geometric trajectory, using Bures geometry to measure movement through representation space and quantum Fisher information to characterize local sensitivity to input factors. We find that learning concentrates local sensitivity on task-relevant factors, and that changing only the prediction target reorganizes this geometry around the corresponding visual factor. More strikingly, representation trajectories become systematically less direct as the learned computation requires higher-order interactions among input factors. This effect persists under matched-performance and training-duration controls and transfers from synthetic vector inputs to residual CNNs on rendered and natural images. Importantly, formation history contains predictive information about the stability of the learned representation: controlling for interaction order, path tortuosity predicts its subsequent drift under continued training and sensitivity to parameter perturbations, whereas endpoint displacement does not. Finally, representation-aware optimization lets us actively shape these trajectories, showing that formation geometry is not only measurable but actionable. Together, these results establish representation formation as a new source of information about learning: its geometry reveals properties of the computation being constructed, predicts subsequent representational stability, and provides a target for intervention during optimization.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Partial Modal Tensor Regression
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: With the rapid development of modern scientific research, tensor data have become increasingly prevalent across a wide range of fields. How to effectively characterize the relationship between tensor predictors and a response while preserving the intrinsic structure of tensor data has therefore become an important problem in high-dimensional statistical analysis. Existing tensor regression methods mainly focus on conditional means or conditional quantiles. When the response distribution is asymmetric, heavy-tailed, or contaminated by outlying observations, the conditional modal provides a robust and interpretable alternative characterization. In this paper, we propose a partial modal tensor regression (PMTR) method. The proposed method constructs the partial modal tensor covariance, which incorporates information on the conditional modal to guide tensor dimension reduction, and subsequently establishes a modal tensor regression model in the reduced tensor space. This strategy alleviates the dimensionality burden caused by direct vectorization while preserving the intrinsic structural information of tensor predictors. Under suitable regularity conditions, we establish the consistency and asymptotic properties of the proposed estimators and employ a data-driven dimension-selection procedure to determine the effective dimension along each tensor mode.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Constrained Gradient Equilibrium: Approachability under Locally Constrained Adversaries
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Gradient equilibrium (GEQ) is a recent framework in online learning that requires the time-averaged gradients along the learner's trajectory to vanish. We study GEQ when the learner is constrained and ask when such an equilibrium remains achievable in an adversarial environment. We first show that constrained GEQ (CGEQ) can be impossible even under simple and slowly varying constraints, motivating imposing local temporal structure on the adversary. We then develop an approachability framework for CGEQ under locally constrained adversaries, and obtain necessary and sufficient characterizations in the spirit of classical Blackwell approachability. Beyond these theoretical characterizations, we provide an algorithmic principle that converts window-wise no-regret learners into CGEQ algorithms under a local feasibility condition with margin. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the resulting algorithms perform strongly in both achieving GEQ and respecting the constraints.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Minimaxity and Admissibility of Bayesian Neural Networks
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a natural probabilistic formulation for inference in deep learning models. Despite their popularity, their optimality has received limited attention through the lens of statistical decision theory. In this paper, we study decision rules induced by deep, fully connected feedforward ReLU BNNs in the normal location model under quadratic loss. We show that, for fixed prior scales, the induced Bayes decision rule is not minimax. We then propose a hyperprior on the effective output variance of the BNN prior that yields a superharmonic square-root marginal density, establishing that the resulting decision rule is simultaneously admissible and minimax. We further extend these results from the quadratic loss setting to the predictive density estimation problem with Kullback--Leibler loss. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings numerically through simulation.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: A Unified Framework for Inference with General Missingness Patterns and Machine Learning Imputation
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Predictions from machine learning (ML) models are increasingly used to impute missing data, but their naive use risks biased inference. Existing methods provide valid inference with ML imputations regardless of prediction quality to enhance efficiency, while they are limited to either simple missing data structures or a missing-completely-at-random assumption. We develop a novel framework for valid statistical inference in Z-estimation problems using ML imputations under a missing-at-random assumption and for general missingness patterns. The method stratifies data by distinct missingness patterns and constructs an estimator by aggregating pattern-specific observed and prediction information. Theoretically, we establish the asymptotic properties and globally optimal aggregation that guarantees efficiency dominance over weighted complete-case analyses (WCCA). Practically, the method affords simple implementations by leveraging existing WCCA software. Extensive simulations validate theoretical results and show clear competitiveness in various scenarios.
