Machine Learning.title: RVPO: Risk-Sensitive Alignment via Variance Regularization
Machine Learning.summary: Current critic-less RLHF methods aggregate multi-objective rewards via an arithmetic mean, leaving them vulnerable to constraint neglect: strong performance in one objective (e.g., correctness) can offset critical failures in others (e.g., safety or formatting). This can mask low-performing "bottleneck" rewards that are necessary for reliable multi-objective alignment. We propose Reward-Variance Policy Optimization (RVPO), a risk-sensitive framework that penalizes variance across rewards during advantage aggregation, and shifts the objective from "maximize sum" to "maximize consistency." Its SoftMin objective can be locally approximated by the mean reward minus an inter-objective variance penalty. We evaluate RVPO on rubric-based medical and scientific reasoning with up to 17 reward signals (Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B) and on tool-calling with rule-based constraints (Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B). RVPO improves overall scores on HealthBench (0.254 vs. 0.207 for GDPO at 14B, averaged across five training seeds). RVPO also maintains competitive accuracy on GPQA-Diamond while reducing late-stage degradation observed in other multi-reward methods.

Machine Learning.title: Interpretable neural equation learning for high-dimensional materials data
Machine Learning.summary: Equation learning seeks to discover compact, interpretable equations from data using various machine-learning techniques. However, few workflows discover and interpret learned equations in sparse, high-dimensional materials datasets. We present nn-EQL, an equation-learning framework that generates candidate equations through iterative training, pruning, and retraining of a neural network with customizable, user-specified neuron-level activation functions. Candidate equations are ranked using a minimum description length (MDL)-inspired score, balancing error and sparsity, and diagnosed to assess term-wise contributions, input-scaled sensitivities, and uncertainties. We demonstrate nn-EQL on standard AI-Feynman benchmarks as well as multiscale high-dimensional materials datasets such as finite-element simulations of heterogeneous materials, and high-throughput experimental thin-film deposition data. nn-EQL integrates with tabular data and high-dimensional data via standard encoder models, learning equations and providing insight into learned terms. Looking forward, integrating physically interpretable representations, multimodal and multi-fidelity data, and adaptive data acquisition could enable equation learning to formulate and test mechanistic hypotheses.

Machine Learning.title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Global Climate Policy Cooperation
Machine Learning.summary: International climate policy requires coordination among countries whose mitigation decisions impose local costs but generate global benefits. Classical game-theoretic and integrated assessment approaches can study these incentives, but typically rely on prescribed behavioural assumptions or equilibrium concepts. Recent work has therefore explored Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning as a way to model climate-policy cooperation as an emergent outcome of repeated strategic interaction. We extend an existing MARL climate framework with a multi-stage negotiation mechanism in which agents propose agreements, accept or reject commitments, and face penalties for non-compliance. This allows us to study how agreement design affects learned mitigation behaviour, compliance, and climate outcomes. In an idealized setting with four homogeneous agents, we find that non-binding agreements do little to overcome free-riding, while moderate non-compliance penalties improve cooperation and reduce warming. However, excessively strong penalties discourage ambitious commitments, revealing a trade-off between enforcement and participation. We position the framework as a methodological contribution for testing agreement design rather than a predictive model of real negotiations.
Machine Learning.comment: Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning: workshop at NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: Finite-Sample Optimal Conformal Prediction Sets under Covariate Shift
Machine Learning.summary:
We study conformal prediction under covariate shift with a known covariate density ratio, seeking prediction sets with minimum expected length under the target distribution. For every calibration sample size, we prove that the rule combining the inverse conditional-density score with randomized weighted conformal calibration minimizes this expected length among all rules valid over the full weighted-exchangeability class.
  We approximate the oracle using quantile and kernel histograms, including forest-weighted estimators, and select estimators and tuning parameters by resampling to estimate calibrated target length. On a bounded response domain, we bound excess length linearly in $L^1$ density error at fixed calibration size, without requiring a uniform positive lower bound on the true density. We also bound selection-pool and resampling errors. Under explicit growth conditions, the selected procedure approaches the same oracle while the calibration size remains fixed.
  Experiments on 36 known-density configurations and four public regression datasets compare coverage, prediction-set length, and runtime with existing methods.
  In targeted low-coverage and strong-shift comparisons, inverse-density selection yields shorter mean sets in most cases and lower mean runtime than the evaluated weighted baselines, with some differences in achieved coverage.

Machine Learning.title: Delta-Matching: Closing the Final Gap of Native 8-bit Training for LLMs
Machine Learning.summary: Reliable FP8 attention remains a barrier to fully native 8-bit large language model training. We derive how forward-backward inconsistencies produce stale delta and empirically show how it distorts training dynamics. Our stale-delta hybrid runs show a modest loss gap at 569M parameters but substantial loss increases and downstream degradation at 1.67B and 5.29B. QK normalization, NoPE (no positional encoding), and lower-learning-rate context extension mitigate or delay degradation without eliminating it. This pattern suggests accumulated optimization error that smaller models and short runs can conceal. We propose Delta-Matching, proving that it restores the softmax gradient's zero-row-sum invariant under the stated numerical assumptions. It enables native block-scaled FP8 in every forward and backward attention-core matmul without architectural changes, smaller global batches, or auxiliary forward outputs. Across tested architectures, scales, and training stages, Delta-Matching matches BF16/FP32 mixed-precision training loss and overall downstream performance. We will release our implementation, trained models, and data recipes (https://jet-ai-projects.github.io/delta-matching).

Machine Learning.title: Test-Time Gradient Guidance of Flow Policies in Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Expressive continuous control policies, such as diffusion and flow models, form the backbone of recent advances in scaling imitation learning for simulated and real robot control. While they are known to scale stably in the supervised imitation learning setting, incorporating them into reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines for policy improvement has proven more difficult. It often requires specialized training objectives or backpropagating through denoising processes, which cause well-known issues with stability and affect scalability. In this paper we study the question of whether simple policy improvement schemes at test time alone, leaving stable supervised policy training intact, can be a competitive alternative which sidesteps these issues. To this end, we propose QGF (Q-Guided Flow), an RL algorithm that performs policy optimization entirely at test time. QGF works by pre-training both a reference flow policy (via a standard behavioral cloning objective) and a value function critic and, at test time, using the value gradient to guide the reference policy to generate higher-value actions without any additional policy learning. Empirically, QGF outperforms prior test-time RL methods on single-task and goal-conditioned offline RL benchmarks with high-dimensional action spaces, and is competitive with state-of-the-art training-time algorithms while being much cheaper to run. Moreover, it exhibits favorable scaling with model size by avoiding the instability of actor-critic training, offering a practical and effective alternative RL algorithm with expressive policies.

Machine Learning.title: An $Ω(T^{3/4})$ lower bound for projection-free online learning with linear minimization oracles
Machine Learning.summary:
This work considers projection-free online learning algorithms with linear minimization oracles for handling the decision set. For Online Frank--Wolfe (OFW), regret upper bounds were already known for specific OFW tunings [Hazan and Kale, 2012, Hazan, 2016] which scaled as $T^{3/4}$ (where $T$ is the horizon length). However, it remained an open question whether the regret of all OFW tunings scaled as $T^{3/4}$.
  We answer that question, proving a universal worst-case regret lower bound $Ω(T^{3/4} m^{-1/4})$ for any projection-free algorithm that makes at most $m$ linear minimization oracle calls per round. The analysis suggests an extended OFW to resort to multiple linear optimizations per round, for which we prove a regret upper bound $O(\max \{ T^{3/4} m^{-1/4}, \sqrt{T} \})$.

Machine Learning.title: Improving Data-Constrained Scaling with Hyperparameter Transfer and Ensembling
Machine Learning.summary: As growing compute budgets outpace the growth of high-quality training data, large language models must be trained with both compute and data constraints in mind. Unfortunately, existing prescriptions for data-constrained scaling suffer from two important limitations. First, past works hold key hyperparameters such as weight decay fixed with scale, despite the fact that optimal hyperparameters vary wildly with model size and number of epochs. Second, past works neglect ensembling, a promising axis for scaling under data constraints. As a surprising consequence, prior prescriptions can lead to loss that increases with compute budget. We address both limitations by fitting power laws that prescribe how to transfer hyperparameters with scale and scaling laws that prescribe how to allocate compute with ensembling. Training on 100M tokens from FineWeb, our recipe reduces validation loss by over 0.15 nats compared to prior recipes, a 14% decrease in perplexity, and achieves monotonic improvements with compute through ensembling. These gains are achieved using prescriptions fit to smaller runs and validated at up to 12$\times$ larger compute budgets.

Machine Learning.title: GViT: Representing Images as Gaussians for Visual Recognition
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce GViT, a supervised classification framework that uses patch-conditioned 2D Gaussian primitives as input tokens for ViT backbones. A ViT-S-sized encoder predicts each primitive's position, scale, orientation, color, and opacity in one forward pass. The same parameters are constrained to reconstruct the image through a differentiable renderer, as well as serve as classifier inputs. During training, classifier-gradient guidance shapes primitive geometry and appearance under an image reconstruction constraint. On ImageNet-1K, GViT-B achieves 76.9% top-1 accuracy, compared with 79.8% for ViT-B/16 trained with the same recipe. Gaussian tokens also provide explicit spatial support for explanation maps. Grad-CAM over Gaussians improves on patch-based Grad-CAM in segmentation and token-deletion probes, while other probe comparisons are comparable to a ViT. A covariance-based foreground diagnostic on the PASCAL VOC segmentation task further measures the geometry learned through supervised guidance. These results establish the feasibility of recognition from renderable Gaussian parameters and characterize how task supervision shapes this inspectable representation.
