Statistical Machine Learning.title: Low-degree polynomials lower bounds for clustering in small dimension
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study the computational limits of clustering $n$ observations drawn from a mixture of $K$ isotropic distributions in $\mathbb R^d$, in the regime where the number $K$ of groups is much larger than the dimension $d$. In this regime, tensor-based procedures recover the partition with a polylogarithmic separation between the centers, but they require a sample size that is a large and non-explicit polynomial of $dK$, whereas the existing low-degree lower bounds only show that $n$ must be larger than $dK^2$. We introduce a mixture of $2K$ product Bernoulli distributions on $\{0,1\}^d$, with $K=(d+1)^m$, whose centers are built from a dual BCH code. This construction ensures that the moment tensors of the observations coincide with those of the uniform distribution on $\{-1,1\}^d$ up to the order $2m+1$. For any fixed $m$, we establish a low-degree polynomial lower bound showing that clustering is hard as long as the separation $Δ$ satisfies $Δ^2\ll(K^2d^{3/2}/n)^{1/(2m+2)}\wedge\sqrt d$, up to polylogarithmic factors. In particular, with a polylogarithmic separation, low-degree polynomials require $n\gtrsim K^2d^{3/2}$ observations, up to polylogarithmic factors. Through a Gaussianization argument, this hardness carries over, in the sense of reductions, to isotropic Gaussian mixtures. Our proof relies on a family of polynomials of the observations, indexed by bipartite graphs, which is almost orthonormal. The moments of these polynomials are governed by the number of solutions of polynomial systems over the finite field $\mathbb F\_{d+1}$ that are induced by the BCH code, and the crux of our analysis is to connect the combinatorial structure of the bipartite graphs with the structure of the solution sets of these systems.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Optimal Experiments for Partial Causal Effect Identification
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Causal queries are often only partially identifiable from observational data, and experiments that could tighten the resulting bounds are typically costly. We study the problem of selecting, prior to observing experimental outcomes, a cost-constrained subset of experiments that maximally tightens bounds on a target query. We formalize this as the max-potency problem, where epistemic potency measures the worst-case reduction in bound width guaranteed by an experiment, and show that this problem is NP-hard via a reduction from 0-1 knapsack. Building on the polynomial-programming framework of Duarte et al. (2023), we give a general procedure for evaluating epistemic potency in discrete settings. To control the super-exponential search space, we introduce two graphical pruning criteria that depend only on the causal graph and the query: a novel path-interception rule that exploits district structure to certify zero potency in linear time, and an identifiability check based on the ID algorithm. On Erdos-Renyi random graphs and 11 bnlearn benchmark networks, the two criteria together prune 50-88% of candidate experiments on average without solving a single polynomial program. For the general subset search, we show that ID-pruned experiments are combinatorially inert, yielding a super-exponential reduction in the number of subsets evaluated. We close with an end-to-end demonstration on observational NHANES data, selecting optimal experiments for estimating the effect of physical activity on diabetes.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Doubly Robust Deep Kernel Tests for Structured Outcomes
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We propose a test of whether two interventions induce the same outcome distribution when outcomes are structured and high-dimensional, such as images, text and graphs. We represent the interventional distributions as mean embeddings on learned deep features, such that the treatment effect is a doubly robust representation of the difference in mean embeddings. Our test, DR-KTE-Deep, optimises the learned features so as to maximise an estimated power criterion on this treatment effect representation. To motivate our learning objective, we show that the power criterion characterises the asymptotic signal-to-noise ratio of the test under fixed alternatives, and we derive a uniform finite-sample bound for its regularised estimate. We show that, with the learned kernel fixed, a held-out test is asymptotically valid under the null given suitable nuisance-estimation rates. Empirically, DR-KTE-Deep achieves substantially higher power than fixed and bandwidth-optimised kernel baselines across image, text and graph outcomes, while maintaining well-calibrated Type-I error.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Reliable probability estimates are critical in many machine learning applications, yet modern classifiers are often poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration provides a simple and widely used solution, but the large number of proposed methods, combined with small-scale and inconsistent evaluations, makes it difficult to determine which approaches are truly effective in practice. We introduce a large-scale, standardized benchmark for post-hoc calibration, covering nearly 2000 experiments across tabular and computer vision tasks, including binary, multiclass, and large-scale classification settings. Our benchmark aggregates predictions from a diverse set of classical models, modern deep learning architectures, and foundation models, and provides unified, reproducible implementations of dozens of calibration methods within a common evaluation framework. We argue that Post-Hoc Improvement (PHI) in proper scoring rules offers a principled alternative to traditional calibration error estimators for comparing post-hoc methods, capturing both calibration quality and potential degradation to the model's predictive performance. Using this framework, we conduct the most comprehensive empirical study of post-hoc calibration to date. Our results reveal consistent patterns across domains: smooth calibration functions outperform binning-based approaches, dedicated multiclass methods are essential in high-dimensional settings, and generic machine learning models are not competitive without calibration-specific design. To facilitate future research, we release all data, code, and evaluation tools, providing a plug-and-play benchmark for developing and comparing calibration methods.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Rènyi-Regularized Flow-Based Variational Inference for Bayesian Calibration
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Variational inference with normalizing flows provides a flexible posterior approximation for Bayesian model calibration, but struggles when the posterior has several modes separated by regions of low probability mass. We study this behavior in a two-parameter twin experiment and regularize the variational objective. Under Gaussian observation errors and a Gaussian prior, the corresponding minimization objective is the expected Tikhonov calibration objective minus the differential entropy of the approximating distribution. However, the expected Tikhonov term favors concentration near one of the modes, while entropy maximization does not guarantee multimodality. We introduce a regularization term based on Rényi divergence that encourages the approximate posterior to cover the prior support. In the connected bimodal case, a flow approximation represents both modes; in the case with well-separated modes, the flow and Gaussian mixture frequently miss one mode. The introduced regularization reduces the near-collapse fraction from 50% to 25%. While the regularization improves mode coverage in this experiment, it changes the Bayesian variational objective, introduces a trade-off in approximation accuracy, and does not provide a general solution to mode collapse.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Physics-Guided Flow Matching: A Generative AI Framework for Global Total Electron Content Forecasting
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Accurate forecasting of global total electron content (TEC) is important for space weather monitoring and the reliable operation of satellite communication and navigation systems. We propose a physics-guided generative artificial intelligence (AI) framework for day-ahead global TEC forecasting. The framework builds on flow matching, which learns to gradually transform samples from an initial distribution into new samples that share the statistical characteristics of the target data. The proposed model incorporates ionospheric dynamics described by a partial differential equation (PDE) into this transformation process, guiding the changes between initial and target samples using physical knowledge. The model further combines the physical dynamics with statistical patterns captured from data to learn this transformation, adaptively adjusting their relative contributions at each location. The model is trained and evaluated using one year of global TEC data generated by the Thermosphere Ionosphere Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIEGCM). The results demonstrate that our model improves both spatial and temporal forecasting accuracy over representative benchmarks, including statistical, deep learning, and generative AI methods at all lead times and across latitudes. The average root mean square error (RMSE) is 39.2% lower than that of ConvLSTM and 23.8% lower than that of the same framework without physical guidance. The learned contribution weights vary systematically with latitude and across geographic locations, showing how the physical contribution changes across the forecast domain. These findings demonstrate that explicit physical guidance improves generative forecasts of global TEC and highlight the value of incorporating physical dynamics into generative AI modeling.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Is Your LLM Relay Serving What It Claims? A low-cost and high-power test for LLM Relay Auditing
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Relay and reseller APIs have become a common way to access large language models (LLMs), yet users cannot directly verify whether they receive the models they request and pay for. This opacity motivates LLM relay auditing, but existing methods struggle to combine low cost, robustness to benign deployment changes, and statistically interpretable decisions under black-box access. To address these limitations, we propose distributional fingerprint auditing (DFA), a statistical method that requires only textual responses from suspect and trusted reference endpoints. DFA repeatedly queries semantically simple finite-choice probes and uses the resulting categorical response distributions to construct endpoint fingerprints. It compares the suspect and reference fingerprints probe by probe and aggregates the resulting evidence using the Cauchy combination test, yielding an approximate endpoint-level $p$-value for audit decisions at a prespecified nominal significance level. Using registered fingerprints of candidate models, a likelihood-based formulation further supports model attribution under full substitution and joint estimation of substitute identity and substitution ratio under constant-ratio mixed routing. Our benchmark includes 16 proprietary and open-weight LLMs from 10 model families. Across 240 ordered full-substitution pairs, DFA achieves high detection rates at a nominal significance level of $α=0.05$, using five probes and 250 relay requests per audit with stored reference fingerprints. Configuration overrides can lead to rejection even when the served model remains unchanged, with effects varying across models and configurations. Simulations based on stored empirical fingerprints demonstrate accurate model attribution and estimate substitution ratios, with estimation error decreasing as the audit budget increases.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Online gas classification at the edge
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Field applications in chemical sensing, from portable safety monitors to mobile robots, require models that are lightweight, fast to respond, and can be recalibrated from limited labelled data. Current gas classification pipelines assume controlled sampling cycles and offline feature extraction, and rely on computationally expensive models. With a few thousand neurons and sub-milliwatt power consumption, insects reliably classify odours in open environments. Inspired by the insect olfactory system, we present a neural network architecture that classifies raw sensor array readings using a sparse, high-dimensional binary representation. We evaluate it on random sequences of single gases and binary mixtures, introducing new samples dynamically and classifying gas identity from the transient sensor response. In this setting, the architecture out-performs a linear \gls{svm} on gas mixtures and matches an optimised non-linear \gls{svm}, while maintaining online class-level frequency estimates that distinguish familiar from novel stimuli. It relies exclusively on binary weights and Hebbian-based local learning, remaining computationally lightweight and well suited to ultra-low-power neuromorphic processors. We demonstrated the network on-chip with a hazardous gas detection experiment running on the mixed-signal neuromorphic chip TEXEL. The on-chip classifier yielded an accuracy of 74.6\% while running at 482 $\unit{\nano\joule}$ per inference and 27 \unit{\micro\watt} of static-power.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Intrinsic Information-Theoretic Analysis of ReLU Nets
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Mutual information (MI) is fundamental to representation-learning analysis in deep networks, but in high dimensions MI estimators depend on hyperparameters whose bias often dominates the signal. We show that continuous piecewise-linear (CPWL) networks, including ReLU networks, admit an intrinsic information-theoretic analysis that avoids this pitfall: their inherent partition of the input space into convex linear regions assigns to every input a discrete region label $Π$ alongside the continuous representation $T$ and label $Y$. We introduce a decomposition of the mutual information $I(Y;T)$ into interpretable geometric terms. We show that the dominant term, the *routing information* $I(Y; Π)$, admits an estimable plug-in estimator, that in the well-sampled regime, approximates a population lower bound on the joint information $I(Y; Π, T)$. When the partition saturates, a functional-equivalence quotient collapses regions implementing the same linear operator and restores informativeness; this extension has a single bounded, dimensionless parameter, which is reported through the quotient's compression ratio. The routing estimator agrees strongly with three established MI baselines applied to the same networks and data. The functional quotient recovers informative estimates in the regime bordering the well-sampled and under-sampled regime. We provide a framework for analysing the internal information geometry of CPWL networks, grounded in their inherent piecewise-linear structure rather than in external discretisation.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Non-asymptotic Estimation of Sparse Partial Correlation via Joint Partial Regression
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Partial correlation analysis is widely used in modern multivariate analysis. However, prior methods lack non-asymptotic guarantees and have slow asymptotic estimation rates. We present a method for simultaneously estimating sparse high-dimensional partial correlation matrices and inverse covariance with non-asymptotic rates. The method is a two-stage estimation which exploits the connection between the inverse covariance matrix and linear regression estimation method while enforcing positive semi-definiteness simultaneously. An efficient proximal splitting algorithm for numerically computing the estimate is also derived, and we provide a fast implementation of the algorithm. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated on both synthetic and real-world data.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Boundary Geometry Determines Optimal Shallow ReLU Approximation under Weighted Coefficient Constraints
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study how boundary geometry affects $L^q$ approximation by shallow ReLU neural networks on convex bodies $K\subset\mathbb R^d$. The target classes are unit balls of weighted variation spaces that can enlarge classical spaces by incorporating domain geometry into constraints on output coefficients. We establish upper and lower bounds for arbitrary convex bodies and determine the optimal polynomial approximation exponents for all planar convex bodies and their products with polytopes, including cubes and circular cylinders. For $C^2$ convex bodies, we determine the optimal exponents in a dimension-dependent range of $q$ extending beyond $2$. When all principal curvatures are positive, the result extends to every finite $q\ge2$. For these classes, the dependence of the optimal exponent on the domain is captured by a single geometric growth exponent associated with small boundary caps. We also identify sharp weight thresholds for retaining the classical approximation exponent and improve previous weights on Euclidean balls while preserving the classical $L^2$ approximation rate. When the target is given as a finite ReLU network, the upper bounds can be realized by a compressed network using only the original neurons, without increasing the weighted coefficient sum. These results show that boundary geometry can change the optimal exponent even when dimension, error norm, and weighting rule are fixed.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Joint Distributional Copula Regression for Insurance Claim Frequency and Severity via Boosting
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: In this paper, we propose a model-based boosting approach for fitting structured additive distributional copula regression models with bivariate responses, focusing particularly on the joint modeling of claim frequency and claim severity. The proposed approach is based on generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS), which extend the general idea of GAMs by allowing multiple parameters of a response distribution, rather than only its conditional mean, to depend on covariates. The model is therefore intrinsically interpretable at the level of its additive predictors, providing greater transparency and auditability than black-box alternatives. We evaluate the proposed framework using synthetic and real-world data. We demonstrate its ability to recover the underlying covariate effects and dependence structure, identify informative variables, and achieve competitive predictive performance relative to benchmark models. We also illustrate how the fitted model can be interpreted.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: ProxyGuard: Direct Reliability Inference for Randomized Data Release Mechanisms with Shared Targets
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Researchers often choose a proxy dataset from many releases, transformations, or seeds. Search can make an invalid release appear adequate, while one adequate release does not establish that its generator is reliable. ProxyGuard controls both errors using prespecified bounded risks and a sealed target set. Named-release mode corrects for multiplicity and certifies specific releases. Direct shared-target mode evaluates independent mechanism draws on a common target, lower-bounds their favorable-score rate, and subtracts a bound on favorable scores contributed by invalid releases. Conditional on the target, release scores are independent, yielding a finite-sample mechanism-reliability guarantee without independent target batches or assumptions on release-level $p$-value dependence. We show that the mean-only penalty is sharp and derive a smooth-score certificate with additive target concentration. In a registered three-requirement study, direct mode raises power from $5.6\%$ to $64.2\%$ at reliability $0.95$, while named mode remains stronger under high-signal evidence. Prospective audits span full-pipeline Rice--TVAE, which retrains on every draw, and a non-tabular text mechanism.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Doubly Robust Alignment for Large Language Models
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: This paper studies reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for aligning large language models with human preferences. While RLHF has demonstrated promising results, many algorithms are highly sensitive to misspecifications in the underlying preference model (e.g., the Bradley-Terry model), the reference policy, or the reward function, resulting in undesirable fine-tuning. To address model misspecification, we propose a doubly robust preference optimization algorithm that remains consistent when either the preference model or the reference policy is correctly specified (without requiring both). Our proposal demonstrates superior and more robust performance than state-of-the-art algorithms, both in theory and in practice. The code is available at https://github.com/DRPO4LLM/DRPO4LLM

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Two-sample comparison through additive tree models for density ratios
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: The ratio of two densities provides a direct characterization of their differences. We consider the two-sample comparison problem by estimating this ratio given i.i.d. observations from two distributions. To this end, we propose additive tree models for density ratio estimation along with efficient algorithms using a new loss function, the balancing loss. The loss allows tree-based models to be trained using several algorithms originally designed for supervised learning, such as forward-stagewise optimization and gradient boosting. Moreover, the balancing loss resembles an exponential family kernel, and it can serve as a pseudo-likelihood with conjugate priors. This property enables generalized Bayesian inference on the density ratio using backfitting samplers designed for Bayesian additive regression trees (BART). Our Bayesian strategy provides uncertainty quantification for the inferred density ratio, which is critical for applications involving high-dimensional and data-limited distributions with potentially substantial uncertainty. We further show connections of the balancing loss to the exponential loss in binary classification and to the variational form of f-divergence, particularly the squared Hellinger distance. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed boosting algorithms achieve high accuracy at low computational cost, and that the Bayesian additive tree is competitive in accuracy while additionally providing uncertainty quantification, which the compared estimators do not offer. Finally, we demonstrate its application to assessing the quality of generative models for microbiome compositional data.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: LLM knowledge for improved Out-of-Distribution Tabular Prediction - A Cross-Validated Regularisation Approach
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Prediction models degrade when the deployment population differs from the one used to train them, and training data cannot say which feature-response relationships will transfer. Expert elicitation is slow and unscalable. We ask whether coefficient priors elicited from large language models (LLMs) improve out-of-distribution (OOD) prediction as the shrinkage target of a regularised regression instead of zero, across five tabular datasets split on real covariates, selecting providers and prior structures by source-domain cross-validation alone. The priors help on four of five datasets, by up to 7.9% OOD mean squared error, and ten of twenty-four prior-informed results resolve the mean improvement at conventional confidence; single-deployment intervals are much wider. On classification the gain is in probabilistic accuracy, not ranking, and control tests with corrupted priors attribute the benefit to feature-specific content rather than scale. Two findings temper this. Variation across candidate priors exceeds the average benefit, yet cross-validation margins fall below their own noise, so selection avoids the worst prior rather than finding the best. On three datasets the prior improves in-domain accuracy as much as out-of-domain, making it better regularisation than shift correction. Only where the training data are large enough that the in-domain gain disappears does elicited knowledge demonstrably improve transfer. Code, priors and results: https://github.com/hugohammer/llm-priors-ood.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Indirect and noisy observations are difficult to invert when the forward operator smooths out the unknown signal. In this case, the unstable modes are precisely the modes that the data reveals least, thus the success of any reconstruction method depends on how prior information interacts with the geometry of the operator across regularity scales. Diffusion priors have become ubiquitous for such problems; however, the current theory still does not determine when a learned score remains informative under ill-posed forward operators. In this paper, we study posterior diffusion for linear inverse problems on Hilbert scales and derive a stability theory under an explicit score-amplification condition. Under a smoothing condition on the forward map, a source condition on the truth, and weak-norm control of score error, we derive non-asymptotic recovery bounds in \(\Hs^s\) that separate observation noise, score approximation, and reverse-time discretization. These bounds give a recoverable regularity threshold determined jointly by operator smoothing, truth regularity, score regularity, and the posterior correction. The threshold specifies the Hilbert-scale norms \(\Hs^s\) in which weak-norm score error remains controlled after propagation through the posterior reverse dynamics. For larger regularity indices \(s\), the inverse geometry magnifies the same error, and the Hilbert-scale recovery estimate no longer gives uniform stability. We also prove that a posterior correction adapted to the forward operator improves stability relative to isotropic guidance in the regularity ranges where the smoothing action of the forward map matters most. The recovery estimates give a regularity-sensitive theory of posterior diffusion and show how learned score error, operator smoothing, and reconstruction norm jointly determine the stable range predicted by the analysis.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Generative Refinement Learning for Temporal Interpolation in Scientific Machine Learning
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Computationally expensive simulations and real-world observations often provide data at a lower temporal resolution than downstream tasks require. Averaging observations at fixed grid points can introduce errors, and motion estimates alone do not determine how the physical field values change. In this work, we study whether learning to correct a simple numerical interpolation improves the reconstruction of intermediate scientific fields. Our model, interpolative FLow EXpert (iFLEX), first estimates the missing field by taking a weighted average of the two observations at each grid point, giving more weight to the observation closer to the requested time. During training, subtracting this estimate from an observed intermediate field gives the residual that a conditional diffusion model learns to generate. Both observations condition the model, together with the target time, the interval between observations, and available physical parameters. To reconstruct an unobserved intermediate field, the generated residual is added to the weighted average. We evaluate iFLEX on Navier-Stokes Kraichnan turbulence, Shanghai radar precipitation, and sea surface temperature. Across these datasets, iFLEX achieves lower reconstruction error than the evaluated baselines, including optical-flow and diffusion models developed for video frame interpolation in computer vision. In a controlled turbulence comparison at a Reynolds number of 36,000, learning the residual reduces relative Frobenius norm error from about 13.7 for direct field generation to 10.5, with the diffusion backbone and training setup held fixed. Code is available at https://github.com/paulpuren/iflex.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: Accepted by Transactions on Machine Learning Research

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Momentum in large-batch training: Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, Nesterov improves data efficiency
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study when and how momentum improves large-batch training in the one-pass regime, using power-law kernel regression as a tractable setting. We first characterize stochastic stability through the \emph{critical learning rate}, defined as the largest learning rate for stable training, and obtain $η_{\mathrm{SGD}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim 1$, $η_{\mathrm{Polyak}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim \min\{1,B(1-β)\}$, and $η_{\mathrm{Nesterov}}^{\mathrm{crit}}\eqsim \min\{1,B^q(1-β)\}$, where $B$ is the batch size, $β\in[0,1)$ is the momentum factor, and \(q>1\) is the capacity exponent governing spectral decay. Within the stable region, we derive scaling laws for the full risk dynamics, capturing the progression from an early transient through power-law decay to a noise floor. We then optimize the final-step risk under a fixed data budget, obtaining a three-regime phase diagram that reveals how the benefits of momentum change with batch size. Notably, Polyak enlarges the critical batch size, the largest batch size preserving the optimal small-batch data-scaling exponent, thereby allowing fewer sequential updates without sacrificing data efficiency. In contrast, Nesterov improves the optimal data-scaling exponent in the large-batch regime through look-ahead-induced suppression of noise amplification. Experiments on PLK regression quantitatively support the theoretical scaling predictions, while neural-network experiments provide qualitative evidence for the predicted batch-size dependence and stability behavior.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: 63 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Revised proofs; added neural-network experiments

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Conservative Dueling Bandits: Preference Learning under Baseline Constraints
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Contextual dueling bandits learn from pairwise comparisons, the same feedback used to fine-tune language models from human preferences. Standard algorithms explore aggressively and can show users two poor options. We study conservative contextual dueling bandits, which require that, at every round, the cumulative score of the better displayed item stay above a $(1-α)$ fraction of a trusted baseline's. An item's score is its probability of beating the best available item, so the constraint depends only on utility differences and needs no absolute rewards. This also changes how safety can be certified: we show that transferring the safety test of the conservative bandit algorithm CLUCB unchanged can incur linear regret, even when the baseline's utilities are known exactly. For linear utilities, we develop MaxInP-BC, which certifies scores through utility gaps and, when it must fall back, pairs the baseline with an informative partner so that fallback rounds still drive learning. It is safe with high probability at all times, with regret $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{T}/κ)$ plus an additive cost of conservatism that does not grow with the horizon. For general utility classes, we develop BTIGW-BC, which turns the guarantee of an online logistic-regression oracle into cumulative safety certificates. It is safe at all times, makes finitely many fallbacks, and has sublinear regret whenever the oracle's logistic regret is sublinear. In experiments, both satisfy the constraint, which their unconstrained counterparts often violate, at a moderate cost in regret.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Kähler landscapes for complex neural network descents and guarantees including a search and destroy of the Calabi-Yau manifold
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study landscapes for complex-parameterized networks. Our approach is motivated with an information-theoretic manifold perspective of the parameter and via classical optimization guarantees although of complex geometric variety such as through Dolbeault asymptotics. The descent path admits a Kähler information metric under a cross-entropy via the Wirtinger Hessian on the log-likelihood potential. We restrict attention to a descent update rule with natural gradient descent via a differentiated loss scaled by the inverse metric, so the descent path remains in the holomorphic tangent bundle. We emphasize Calabi-Yau information manifolds which profane theoretical guarantees via an ill-curvature-conditioned, or lack thereof, landscape. We focus on Calabi-Yau metrics specifically in a non-compact setting with a global potential, so defined geometrically rather than invoking the topological requirements of the Calabi conjecture. In non-compact settings, we can write the metric determinant with respect to a background in terms of a function, pluriharmonic or real. Using Yau's Liouville theorem, we get a partial eigenvalue blow-up effect. In an empirical setting, a Ricci-flat metric will not form, but a blow-up can be a local condition and can hold empirically on open sets even partially in generalized Kähler cases due to lower bounds on the Ricci potential. Moreover, it has been discovered that negative curvature subverts the loss landscape, specifically sectional curvature, so we expand on this and draw interconnections to negative-definite Ricci curvature. Our arguments primarily exist via geometric modality, although we establish roots in deep learning theory such as through asymptotics at initialization and connections through failure modes of neural network guarantees under vanishing and negative Ricci curvature.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: An Asymptotic Theory of Chain-of-Thought in In-Context Learning
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become a widely used mechanism for eliciting multi-step reasoning in large language models by generating intermediate reasoning steps at inference time. Yet the scaling behavior of generalization with CoT depth remains poorly understood. To address this question, we study a theoretically solvable model of CoT for in-context weight prediction in linear regression, where test-time reasoning is represented as an iterative refinement of the weight-parameter estimate. Using tools from random matrix theory under high-dimensional asymptotics, we derive an exact formula for the generalization error as a function of reasoning depth, pretraining data amount, and context length. Our analysis reveals a sharp phase transition separating exponential and polynomial improvement, saturation, and overthinking, and characterizes how the optimal reasoning depth scales. We further show that deeper reasoning is most effective with sufficiently rich pretraining and in-context information, whereas limited pretraining or context makes longer reasoning prone to error amplification or saturation. We also validate these predictions through experiments on fully learned linear attention and softmax attention models. Our results provide a unified theoretical account of how test-time CoT depth affects generalization.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: PDE-Based Bounds on Optimal Exponents in Active Simple Hypothesis Testing
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We present general upper and lower bounds on the optimal error exponent for the Active Simple Hypothesis Testing (ASHT) problem. ASHT has been extensively studied across diverse fields including Information Theory, Bandits, and Operations Research, a precise characterization of this optimal exponent has remained elusive. This work combines a recent Partial Differential Equation (PDE) characterization of the optimal exponent by Vijayan (2025) with the comparison principle of viscosity solutions of Hamilton-Jacobi PDEs. This leads to bounds that are parametrized by convex functions, sets and lower Hamiltonian relaxations, a flexibility that generalizes many known results in the literature.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Deep Bayesian Approaches for Interpretable Nonlinear Structural System Identification
Statistical Machine Learning.summary:
System identification, namely the inference of mathematical representations of dynamical systems from measured data, is fundamental to engineering diagnostics, prognostics, and decision-making. Bayesian filtering offers a principled framework for probabilistic state estimation but traditionally relies on prescribed transition and observation models. Recent advances in deep Bayesian filtering address this limitation by embedding learnable representations within probabilistic state-space formulations, enabling data-driven identification of unknown dynamics while retaining physical structure and uncertainty-aware inference.
  This tutorial provides a systematic introduction to deep Bayesian filtering for nonlinear structural system identification, focusing on the interplay between learned dynamics, physical inductive biases, and posterior inference. The Deep Markov Model serves as a data-driven reference, while the Physics-guided Deep Markov Model (PgDMM) and Neural Extended Kalman Filter (Neural EKF) illustrate complementary approaches based on amortized variational inference and differentiable Kalman filtering, respectively. Their capabilities are examined through dynamic state estimation and joint dynamic state and parameter estimation on a three-dimensional shear-frame benchmark with hysteretic Bouc-Wen connections and sparse acceleration measurements. The results highlight important distinctions between measurement-conditioned reconstruction and open-loop forecasting, demonstrate how physical structure can improve latent-state interpretability without necessarily ensuring predictive fidelity, and reveal differences in the robustness of response and parameter estimation. Practical guidelines for model construction, training, evaluation, and deployment are provided, together with an outlook on remaining challenges in uncertainty calibration, identifiability, and real-world validation.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Wasserstein approximation of measures via orthogonal frames: statistical and computational complexities
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Dimension-reduction methods such as PCA identify a subspace capturing most of the variation in the data, but not a distinguished basis within it. Selecting a basis in which the samples are sparsely represented is a recurring task in unsupervised learning, addressed by methods in factor analysis, dictionary learning, and subspace clustering. We pose this task as Wasserstein approximation of the data distribution by measures supported on the axes of an orthogonal frame, which, in turn, reduces to a nonsmooth optimization problem over the orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(d)$. We show that, under mild assumptions, both empirical risk minimizers and a locally initialized stochastic gradient method recover the population-optimal frame at the near-parametric rate $\widetilde{O}_d(n^{-1/2})$, where $n$ is the sample size. The main difficulty is that, although the population objective is smooth, the empirical objective is not-this mismatch precludes standard covering arguments. We overcome this issue by replacing Lipschitz continuity of the empirical gradient with a coarsely Lipschitz bound, a tool that may be of independent interest. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Nuclear Norm-Regularized Bayesian Matrix Completion
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Nuclear-norm-regularized least squares is a standard approach to matrix completion, but it yields only a point estimate. Its Bayesian counterpart, a prior combining the nuclear norm with a Frobenius-norm term, gives a strongly log-concave though nonsmooth posterior when the noise precision is known. In practice the precision is unknown, and placing a truncated Jeffreys prior on it makes the joint posterior neither log-concave nor smooth. To our knowledge, we give the first sampler for this model with an explicit non-asymptotic guarantee: its output is within a prescribed total-variation or Wasserstein distance of the posterior on the matrix after a number of steps polynomial in the matrix dimensions and the reciprocal of the target accuracy. The sampler never targets a continuous distribution that is not strongly log-concave. It discretizes the precision onto a grid, estimates its posterior by thermodynamic integration along the tilted conditional posteriors of the matrix, and bounds the error this propagates to the posterior on the matrix. The approach applies whenever non-log-concavity is confined to a bounded scalar hyperparameter and the conditional distributions are strongly log-concave with smooth-plus-Lipschitz potentials. Our result establishes feasibility; the polynomial complexity is not intended as a practical algorithm at current problem scales.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: BRIDGE: An Acceptance Gate to Block False Improvements in Model Updates, with a Retrospective Clinical Evaluation
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Models are updated repeatedly, and an update that looks better on validation data but not on new data is a false improvement that can misguide clinical decisions. The naive rule accepts every positive validation gain and is optimistic when the same data choose and judge the update. BRIDGE is a model-agnostic acceptance gate that decides each update from predictions and the available labels, with fixed settings. Each fold of the data judges the update chosen on the other folds (cross-fitting) to reduce selection bias; acceptance requires the gain's lower bootstrap bound to exceed a margin. The four settings are (A) 11 new datasets, (B) synthetic tasks, (C) 12 retrospective clinical tasks, and (D) 39 supporting datasets. The false-improvement rate falls from 19.1% (naive) to 1.1% (BRIDGE) in (A), 20.7% to 1.7% (B), 20.0% to 0% (C), and 12.5% to 0.5% (D); every 95% confidence interval of the reduction over datasets or tasks excludes zero (not over the clinical sources). An equal-size random draw from the naive acceptances contains more false improvements in (A)-(E) (post hoc, p<0.001). On the OpenML collection (E) of 14 new datasets, the false-improvement rate falls from 25.6% to 1.0%. BRIDGE removes 97% to 100% of the false improvements that the naive rule accepts, and its mean gain per deployed update is 1.8 to 3.1 times the naive rule's. The 95% upper bound on the false-improvement rate is below 5.5%: formal in (B) for independent tasks (3.56%), and conditional on the real data tested (0.33% to 5.40%).
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: 40 pages, 5 figures. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23523984

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Learning Sequential Decisions from Multiple Sources via Group-Robust Markov Decision Processes
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Learning a common policy from multiple source environments requires accounting for cross-source heterogeneity, and the offline setting introduces an additional challenge of limited data coverage. We formulate this problem as a distributionally robust Markov decision process under a shared linear MDP representation with source-specific transition and reward components. The uncertainty set is constructed through feature-wise mixtures of these components, yielding a $d$-rectangular structure that captures cross-source heterogeneity and admits a robust Bellman recursion. Building on this formulation, we develop Group-Robust Pessimistic Value Iteration (GR-PEVI), an offline policy-learning algorithm that combines feature-wise worst-case aggregation with a data-dependent pessimism penalty. Under a robust partial coverage condition, we establish finite-sample suboptimality guarantees for GR-PEVI and extend the analysis to clustered sources, characterizing the trade-off between the statistical gain from pooling similar sources and the approximation error induced by within-cluster heterogeneity. Simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of GR-PEVI, with empirical behavior consistent with the theoretical analysis. We apply GR-PEVI to a multi-source electronic health record study of multiple sclerosis treatment decisions to illustrate its use in a clinical setting.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Algorithmics for Graphical Separation Criteria
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Statistical graphical models are representations of the dependences between the components of a random vector. They encode these dependences via graphical separation criteria. We consider the algorithmic problem of checking separation statements for the various graph classes and separation criteria that have been developed by the community. We establish that all criteria we study can be checked by modular variations of reachability. For all separation criteria but $σ$-separation, this yields a linear-time algorithm. This is effectively the optimal attainable time since loading the graph itself is linear-time in the number of edges in the graph. Using the CIfly framework for deploying modular variations of reachability, we also provide R and Python code implementing our algorithms. We evaluate empirical runtime and scaling behavior in a simulation study.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Second-order Sinkhorn Geometry and $\sqrt{n}$-Inference
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: The Sinkhorn divergence, a debiased form of entropic optimal transport, has been widely used in various scientific disciplines due to its computational and statistical tractability. Unlike the Wasserstein distance, however, the Sinkhorn divergence is not a metric and it does not naturally admit a formal Riemannian structure. These properties are central to many applications of optimal transport methods that utilize interpolation, barycentric averaging, parallel transport or other geometric operations. Recent work addresses these shortcomings by constructing a formal Riemannian tangent space and a metric tensor on the space of probability measures that quadratically approximates the Sinkhorn divergence. In this work, we extend this framework with two major threads of contributions. For a suitable class of finite-smoothness cost functions, we prove Hadamard differentiability of the Sinkhorn metric tensor and we derive the Levi-Civita covariant derivative in this geometry; we then use the covariant derivative to obtain the geodesic and parallel transport equations, each of which amount to an ODE on a fixed Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) with smooth coefficients. Our second contribution is to linearize the solutions to the geodesic and parallel transport equations using standard tools from Banach space ODE theory. We show that under standard regularity conditions these linearizations imply $\sqrt{n}$-limiting Gaussian processes centered at population values for the plugin estimators of the exponential map, the logarithmic map, parallel transport and the induced Sinkhorn distance. Moreover, we show that the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent for all objects mentioned. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first $\sqrt{n}$--limit theorems and bootstrap consistency results for canonical geometric operations in a transport-based geometry on the space of probability measures.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Revenge of Monosemanticity: Neuron Specialization as a New Form of Feature Learning in MLPs
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Understanding how neural networks learn and organize features is central to understanding their behavior. Much existing theory of feature learning has focused on the emergence of a global low-dimensional representation. We show that this picture is incomplete. In regression problems with clustered data, we demonstrate that multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) develop specialized neurons: individual neurons become strongly aligned with specific features relevant to a particular region of the input space. A substantial fraction of these neurons exhibit monosemanticity: they activate predominantly on inputs from the corresponding cluster. Thus, rather than learning a single global low-dimensional representation, MLPs learn a collection of local low-dimensional representations. Furthermore, we show that this ability to specialize gives MLPs a provable data-efficiency advantage over feature-learning methods based on a global low-dimensional representation.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Advantage of Sample Complexity in Quantum PAC Learning Requires Inverse Access to State-Preparation Unitaries
Statistical Machine Learning.summary:
Whether quantum computation can reduce the amount of data required for conventional machine learning is a central problem in quantum machine learning. In probably approximately correct (PAC) learning, a learner receives training examples sampled from an unknown probability distribution. Quantum PAC learning extends this framework by allowing access to quantum examples, which are quantum states that coherently encode this distribution, or to unitaries that prepare quantum examples, with or without inverse access. When only copies of quantum examples are available, the optimal worst-case sample complexity asymptotically matches that of classical learning. In contrast, access to both a preparation unitary and its inverse can improve the accuracy dependence of query complexity. However, it has remained open whether access to the preparation unitary alone suffices for this improvement.
  In this work, we resolve this question by determining the optimal query complexity with forward-only access, taking the worst case over compatible preparation unitaries and their dimensions. In both realizable and agnostic PAC learning, this complexity matches, up to constant factors, the optimal sample complexity achievable with classical examples or copies of quantum examples. To prove these results, we construct, for any algorithm with forward-only access, a simulator that approximates the algorithm's Haar-averaged output state using as many copies of the prepared state as the algorithm makes queries. These results show that inverse access is essential for the known improvement in accuracy dependence in this worst-case setting. Beyond PAC learning, our reduction provides a general tool for transferring lower bounds for state copies to query lower bounds for forward-only access to the corresponding preparation unitaries.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: 37 pages, 3 figures. Added explanatory figures, simplified parts of the proofs, and revised the exposition. Main results unchanged

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Improved Regret Bounds for Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound in Bayesian Optimization
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: This paper addresses the Bayesian optimization problem (also referred to as the Bayesian setting of the Gaussian process bandit), where the learner seeks to minimize the regret under a function drawn from a known Gaussian process (GP). Under a Matérn kernel with a certain degree of smoothness, we show that the Gaussian process upper confidence bound (GP-UCB) algorithm achieves $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ cumulative regret with high probability. Furthermore, our analysis yields $O(\sqrt{T \ln^2 T})$ regret under a squared exponential kernel. These results fill the gap between the existing regret upper bound for GP-UCB and the best-known bound provided by Scarlett (2018). The key idea in our proof is to capture the concentration behavior of the input sequence realized by GP-UCB, enabling a more refined analysis of the GP's information gain.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: 36 pages, NeurIPS 2025. In v3, I added a supplementary proof of the local quadratic condition and corrected typos and minor errors. No other changes were made

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Orlicz-Sobolev with Musielak: An Efficient Regularization Approach for Graph-based IPM
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study the Sobolev IPM problem for probability measures supported on a graph metric space, where critic function is constrained to lie within the unit ball defined by Sobolev norm. Sobolev IPM is intrinsically coupled with $L^p$ geometric structure within its definition, limiting its ability to incorporate other prior geometry beyond the $L^p$ paradigm. Conversely, the classic optimal transport is flexible, easy to adapt to various geometric structures by simply changing its ground cost. An important example is Orlicz-Wasserstein (OW) which utilizes \emph{Orlicz} geometric structure to generalize the $L^p$ within the standard $p$-order Wasserstein, and remarkably play a vital role to advance machine learning methodologies. Inspired by recent advantages of OW, in this work, we leverage a specific class of convex functions for Orlicz geometry to mitigate such limitation for Sobolev IPM, and propose the generalized Sobolev IPM (GSI). Our GSI approach encompasses Sobolev IPM as a special case while accommodating diverse geometric priors beyond $L^p$. It however brings up significant computational hurdles that compound those already notoriously inherent in Sobolev IPM. To address these challenges, we theoretically establish a novel connection between \emph{Orlicz-Sobolev} norm and \emph{Musielak} norm which facilitates a novel efficient regularization for GSI. By further exploiting the underlying graph structure, we show that the regularized GSI reduces to a simple univariate optimization problem, achieving notably computational efficiency, enabling its usage in practical applications. We empirically illustrate that the regularized GSI is several-order faster than the popular OW in computation, and its performances compare favorably to other transport baselines for comparing graph-based measures in document classification and topological data analysis.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Interpretable Feature Discovery from Unstructured Data Using LLMs and Statistical Choice Models
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Feature extraction from unstructured data typically relies on opaque embeddings unsuited to interpretable decision-making. Interpretable features, on the other hand, typically require costly, and often infeasible, hand-engineering. Large language models (LLMs) offer a natural bridge, as they can read raw data and describe it in interpretable terms. One could simply ask an LLM to extract features from a large sample of the dataset, but context limitations and diluted attention can lead to unsatisfactory results. We introduce a method that automatically discovers interpretable, decision-relevant features from unstructured data. Our key idea is to perform pairwise comparisons between items, asking an LLM to articulate, in interpretable terms, the features distinguishing each pair. We treat these explanations, or rationales, as data: we develop a statistical choice model that combines these rationales across the comparisons to identify relevant features and estimate per-item, per-feature scores. We first test our method on a synthetic hiring dataset of cover letters with known ground-truth features and show that it significantly outperforms direct LLM feature extraction in feature recovery. We then apply it to the ChangeMyView (Reddit) debate dataset, where it discovers several interpretable features associated with persuasion while reaching predictive accuracy comparable to established baselines. We also show how the same rationales can be used to audit LLM decisions, yielding a holistic score whose decomposition over interpretable features reveals what the LLM rewards.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Sticky Jump Diffusions: A Unifying View of Masked, Continuous, and Hybrid Diffusion
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We introduce sticky jump diffusions (SJDs), continuous-time Markov processes on $\mathbb{R}^d$ whose discrete anchors are token embeddings. In forward time, anchors release their mass at a hazard rate and the released mass diffuses in the continuous ambient space; time reversal couples a score-driven SDE with a sticky jump kernel whose rate and destination are fixed by flux balance with the forward law. We estimate the score and the per-anchor reverse hazards from a single denoising classifier via denoising hazard matching, the hazard analogue of denoising score matching, with simulation-free cross-entropy training. SJD recovers masked diffusion, continuous diffusion, and hybrid diffusion as limits. Its reversal explains features that each family treats as given: the mask of masked diffusion carries no evidence about the source token because the unsticking kernel of every anchor collapses to the same absorbing point; the terminal projection of continuous diffusion is required due to the absence of atoms in its forward marginal, without which flux balance yields no reverse jumps; and the update rules of hybrid diffusion (commit rate, destination, and drift) all follow from flux balance rather than from separate design. Beyond these limits, the unsticking kernel becomes a design space: a cross-position blending corrupts each position toward a blend of its neighbors' clean values or embeddings, turning dependency structure such as spatial locality or a constraint graph into an inductive bias of the corruption itself, and improves over the identity-kernel hybrid on CIFAR-10, Text8, and Sudoku.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Conformal Predictive Distributions for Contextual Order Fulfillment Optimization
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Ship-to-home fulfillment requires a retailer to select a fulfillment location and carrier before the delivery time is known. These decisions often rely on static transit-time estimates, which cannot represent how delivery-time uncertainty varies across orders and fulfillment options. This paper constructs conformal predictive distributions (CPDs) using Conformal Predictive Systems (CPS) for regression and the cross Venn-Abers predictor (CVAP) for multiclass classification, and uses them in a contextual optimization model for fulfillment decisions. The model is solved by contextual sample-average approximation (C-SAA). The regret of each fulfillment decision, its expected cost above that of the best decision, is bounded by forecast error, scenario-evaluation error, and the candidate-generation gap. The forecast term depends on how well calibration residuals or class probabilities represent the current order. On more than five million proprietary order records, CVAP raises exact-day accuracy from 49.5% for the rule-based estimate to 64.1%. Paired with a decision rule that selects a quantile weighting late errors more heavily, the split CPS (SCPS) gives a point estimate that raises late-delivery detection from 3.8% to 79.4%. Residual-based CPS distributions also meet or slightly exceed nominal interval-coverage targets. In decision experiments with a JD.com simulator over six test dates, C-SAA with CVAP lowers mean total cost by 7.1% and C-SAA with the Mondrian CPS (MCPS) lowers it by 6.7%, relative to C-SAA with the original nonconformal forecast. Both cut the late-delivery rate from 5.7% to below 4.0%.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: MAGIC: Multi-task Gaussian process for joint imputation and classification in healthcare time series
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Time series analysis has emerged as an important tool for improving patient diagnosis and management in healthcare applications. However, these applications commonly face two critical challenges: time misalignment and data sparsity. Traditional approaches address these issues through a two-step process of imputation followed by prediction. We propose MAGIC (Multi-tAsk Gaussian Process for Imputation and Classification), a novel unified framework that simultaneously performs class-informed missing value imputation and label prediction within a hierarchical multi-task Gaussian process coupled with functional logistic regression. To handle intractable likelihood components, MAGIC employs Taylor expansion approximations with bounded error analysis, and parameter estimation is performed using EM algorithm with block coordinate optimization supported by convergence analysis. We validate MAGIC through two healthcare applications: prediction of post-traumatic headache improvement following mild traumatic brain injury and prediction of in-hospital mortality within 48 hours after ICU admission. In both applications, MAGIC achieves superior predictive accuracy compared to existing methods. The ability to generate real-time and accurate predictions with limited samples facilitates early clinical assessment and treatment planning, enabling healthcare providers to make more informed treatment decisions.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Efficient Deep Gaussian Process Surrogates via Mini-Batch Latent MAP Estimation
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) are flexible surrogate models for computer experiments with nonstationary response surfaces, but inference over their latent representations remains computationally challenging. Existing methods typically rely on variational inference or Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which impose variational-family assumptions or require costly posterior sampling. We propose the latent maximum-a-posteriori deep Gaussian process (LaMP-DGP), which uses gradient-based optimization to obtain MAP estimates of the latent representations and enables efficient probabilistic prediction through linked-GP calculations. To scale LaMP-DGP to large datasets, we develop a mini-batch optimization algorithm and, under a polynomial mini-batch bias-decay condition, establish a stationarity bound for latent-state optimization that motivates a growing batch-size schedule. Across numerical experiments and real-data analyses, LaMP-DGP provides consistently competitive predictive performance relative to doubly stochastic variational inference, stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and fully Bayesian Vecchia DGP inference. Computationally, LaMP-DGP is substantially faster than the Vecchia MCMC approach while remaining broadly competitive with the stochastic-gradient alternatives. These results position LaMP-DGP as a competitive and computationally efficient alternative for DGP inference. An R package, "LaMPDGP", is available for implementing the proposed method.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: 35 pages including references, 11 pages appendix, 5 figures

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Integral Probability Boundaries
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Bounds based on Integral Probability Metrics (IPMs) are ubiquitous in machine learning and statistics, appearing, e.g., in generalization, alignment, fairness, and privacy. IPMs reduce the discrepancy between two distributions to a single worst-case gap between expectations. This compression is costly: for rare events, safety failures, or under-represented groups, IPM-based bounds are loose or vacuous. We introduce a non-linear generalization of IPMs, which we term Integral Probability Boundaries (IPBs). Unlike IPMs, IPBs provide bounds that are tight at the extremes. We derive their basic properties and present algorithms for estimating them in practically relevant settings. We demonstrate the usage of IPBs in both theoretical and practical applications for alignment, judge-free performance estimation, and fairness, where they enable us to obtain sharp bounds on performance and fairness gaps, e.g., 15 p.p. more precise estimates on fairness gaps for rare groups in a realistic generative modeling task, compared to the state of the art.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: New Multiple Descent Phenomena Induced by Heterogeneous Data
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Modern machine learning models are often trained on large datasets assembled from many different sources, whose statistical properties can differ substantially. Understanding how this heterogeneity affects generalization performance is therefore important for explaining how model performance changes as model size increases. In this work, we study this question in linear random-feature models and show that mixtures of datasets with different covariance structures can give rise to a range of multiple-descent phenomena. We derive exact asymptotic expressions for the test error of each data source in the high-dimensional regime, and show how heterogeneity in covariance scale and spectral structure can introduce additional, group-dependent interpolation thresholds as model size increases. These phenomena arise even with noiseless labels and linear activations, showing that neither label noise nor activation nonlinearity is necessary for multiple-descent. Our results therefore provide a different perspective from classical explanations of multiple descent. More broadly, our results have potential implications for algorithmic fairness by showing that model scaling can affect different data groups unevenly, amplifying disparities in their generalization errors. We validate our theoretical results on synthetic Gaussian mixtures and real-world datasets, including MNIST and CIFAR-10.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: A Connection Between Score Matching and Local Intrinsic Dimension
Statistical Machine Learning.summary:
The local intrinsic dimension (LID) of data is a fundamental quantity in signal processing and learning theory, but quantifying the LID of high-dimensional, complex data has been a historically challenging task. Recent works have discovered that diffusion models capture the LID of data through the spectra of their score estimates and through the rate of change of their density estimates under various noise perturbations. While these methods can accurately quantify LID, they require either many forward passes of the diffusion model or use of gradient computation, limiting their applicability in compute- and memory-constrained scenarios.
  We show that the LID is a lower bound on the denoising score matching loss, motivating use of the denoising score matching loss as a LID estimator. Moreover, we show that the equivalent implicit score matching loss also approximates LID via the normal dimension and is closely related to a recent LID estimator, FLIPD. Our experiments on a manifold benchmark and with Stable Diffusion 3.5 indicate that the denoising score matching loss is a highly competitive and scalable LID estimator, achieving superior accuracy and memory footprint under increasing problem size and quantization level.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: Accepted to the 3rd SPIGM Workshop at NeurIPS 2025

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Finite-Step Geometry of Marginal-Preserving Velocity Fields in Generative Flows
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Generative flows can admit different velocity fields that induce the same continuous marginal evolution but behave differently after numerical discretization. We study this finite-step non-equivalence while keeping the marginal path and numerical method fixed. Projected modified equations characterize the component of local integration error that changes the marginal law and give sufficient conditions for higher marginal convergence order. For affine fixed-shape distributions, we characterize exact finite-step reachability and derive spectral obstructions and sharp nearest-reachable Wasserstein errors. For diffusion probability-flow ODEs, we construct skew-score perturbations that preserve the exact marginal path under exact scores and quantify their leakage under score error. Controlled Gaussian and mixture experiments recover the predicted order, reachability, and obstruction phenomena.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Simulation-Based Inference with Convolutional Maximum Mean Discrepancy for Noisy Data
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Ignoring measurement noise degrades statistical inference. Existing correction techniques are often computationally costly and inefficient. Kernel methods based on maximum mean discrepancy have enabled efficient, likelihood-free inference, but they typically assume clean data. We introduce a framework for inference with samples corrupted by potentially heteroscedastic noise from a known distribution. Central to our method is the convolutional maximum mean discrepancy, which compares distributions after noise convolution and retains metric validity under standard kernel conditions. We establish finite-sample deviation bounds that are unaffected by measurement error and an equivalence between testing under noise and kernel smoothing. Based on this discrepancy, we propose an estimator, establish its consistency and asymptotic normality, and provide an efficient implementation using stochastic gradient descent. We demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our method through simulations and applications in astronomy, anthropometry, and the social sciences. Our method provides a unified, likelihood-free, simulation-based framework for efficient and robust inference for broad classes of problems in noisy data.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Online Learning
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: We study online Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization (DRO), where the ambiguity set is a Wasserstein ball centered at the empirical distribution and evolves with each observation. We formulate each round as a zero-sum game and develop an online distributional best-response algorithm that requires only one projected subgradient step per iteration. Combining regret analysis with measure concentration, we establish explicit, instance-dependent, and high-probability convergence rates to the optimal offline DRO value.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Finite-Sample Optimal Conformal Prediction Sets under Covariate Shift
Statistical Machine Learning.summary:
We study conformal prediction under covariate shift with a known covariate density ratio, seeking prediction sets with minimum expected length under the target distribution. For every calibration sample size, we prove that the rule combining the inverse conditional-density score with randomized weighted conformal calibration minimizes this expected length among all rules valid over the full weighted-exchangeability class.
  We approximate the oracle using quantile and kernel histograms, including forest-weighted estimators, and select estimators and tuning parameters by resampling to estimate calibrated target length. On a bounded response domain, we bound excess length linearly in $L^1$ density error at fixed calibration size, without requiring a uniform positive lower bound on the true density. We also bound selection-pool and resampling errors. Under explicit growth conditions, the selected procedure approaches the same oracle while the calibration size remains fixed.
  Experiments on 36 known-density configurations and four public regression datasets compare coverage, prediction-set length, and runtime with existing methods.
  In targeted low-coverage and strong-shift comparisons, inverse-density selection yields shorter mean sets in most cases and lower mean runtime than the evaluated weighted baselines, with some differences in achieved coverage.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: An $Ω(T^{3/4})$ lower bound for projection-free online learning with linear minimization oracles
Statistical Machine Learning.summary:
This work considers projection-free online learning algorithms with linear minimization oracles for handling the decision set. For Online Frank--Wolfe (OFW), regret upper bounds were already known for specific OFW tunings [Hazan and Kale, 2012, Hazan, 2016] which scaled as $T^{3/4}$ (where $T$ is the horizon length). However, it remained an open question whether the regret of all OFW tunings scaled as $T^{3/4}$.
  We answer that question, proving a universal worst-case regret lower bound $Ω(T^{3/4} m^{-1/4})$ for any projection-free algorithm that makes at most $m$ linear minimization oracle calls per round. The analysis suggests an extended OFW to resort to multiple linear optimizations per round, for which we prove a regret upper bound $O(\max \{ T^{3/4} m^{-1/4}, \sqrt{T} \})$.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Investigating the Early Signatures of Feature Learning in Deep Linear Networks
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Deep neural networks learn data-dependent features, a capacity widely credited for their empirical success. However, explicitly characterizing what features emerge -- and when they improve generalization -- is challenging, since training is nonlinear and non-convex and the data is often anisotropic. Here, we give a closed-form account of feature learning for a deep linear network in a mean-field parameterization, trained by one gradient step from initialization on high-dimensional data carrying a low-dimensional (spiked) signal. In the infinite-width mean-field limit, one step updates each layer's feature kernel by a target-aligned rank-one spike, amplified by both the learning rate and the layer depth. We next assess how these features impact prediction through kernel ridge regression (KRR), finding that KRR on the learned feature kernel yields scalar inflation of the KRR estimator at initialization -- an "anti-shrinkage" mechanism that reinflates task-relevant directions suppressed by ridge, while also amplifying noise. To study when this inflation improves generalization, in the overparameterized proportional limit we derive closed-form expressions for the bias, variance, and generalization errors of these estimators in terms of key macroscopic parameters -- notably the spike strength and spike-target alignment. Crucially, we find that a one-step generalization advantage vanishes for isotropic inputs and appears when both the spike strength and an effective signal-to-noise ratio are sufficiently large, demonstrating that a successful first gradient step both requires and benefits from low-dimensional task structure.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: 92 pages, 7 figures, 16 pages of main text

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Universal Short-Time Fourier Transform: Data-Adaptive Window-Length Selection for Time-Frequency Analysis
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) characterizes the local frequency content of time-varying signals by evaluating the discrete Fourier transform over a sliding analysis window. The STFT is governed by a fundamental resolution trade-off: a short window localizes rapid transients in time at the cost of frequency resolution, whereas a long window resolves closely spaced harmonics at the expense of temporal resolution. The Universal Short-Time Fourier Transform (U-STFT) resolves this trade-off sequentially by modeling the analysis window duration as a data-adaptive state variable that indexes the number of hops included in the current observation interval. At each frame, a bank of candidate window durations is scored using normalized order-three Rényi entropy to quantify joint time-frequency concentration. A window length trellis aggregates the resulting $\mathcal{O}(3^M)$ candidate window schedules with linear complexity per frame, guaranteeing a cumulative mix-loss regret bound of $\mathcal{O}((k+1)\log M)$ relative to any hindsight window schedule with $k$ resolution changes over $M$ frames. By linearity of the Fourier transform, posterior expectation across the candidate bank yields a single spectrum equivalent to an STFT evaluated with a data-adaptive effective window, while an envelope-normalized synthesis stream guarantees exact overlap-add reconstruction. Evaluations on synthetic and marine bioacoustic signals demonstrate adaptive resolution tracking, enhanced spectral concentration, and exact time-domain invertibility.

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Anisotropic Trust Region Warping for Prior-Data Fitted Networks in Bayesian Optimisation
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) replace the hyperparameter refitting of Gaussian Process (GP) surrogates in Bayesian optimisation with a single forward pass, at the cost of a prior that is fixed at meta-training time. We show empirically that a PFN's predictive log-likelihood falls increasingly behind that of a refitted GP as the objective function's lengthscale grows beyond the mode of the PFN's meta-training prior, and that this deficit carries over to optimisation performance. To correct the mismatch without retraining the network, we introduce Anisotropic Trust Region (ATR) warping. Per-dimension lengthscales are estimated by kernel target alignment, and an affine rescaling of the input space maps the objective onto the lengthscale the PFN expects, with a trust region around the anchor determining which observations are retained, leaving the PFN's $\mathcal{O}(d \cdot N^2)$ inference cost unchanged. On functions drawn from a Matérn-3/2 kernel, ATR warping improves optimisation performance of the PFN at both extremes of the lengthscale range. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/Trust-Region-Warping-For-PFNs.
Statistical Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at the 2026 NeurIPS Workshop on Optimization for Machine Learning (OPT). 18 pages, 12 figures

Statistical Machine Learning.title: Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
Statistical Machine Learning.summary: Model discrepancy may prevent a single calibration parameter from reproducing a physical response across the context domain. In addition, uncertainties in observations and contexts affect calibration and must be accounted for and quantified. We construct a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods according to their proximity to a target context. Gaussian localization weights incorporate context uncertainty through covariance inflation, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. A conditional normalizing flow approximates the family of posteriors through amortized variational inference. Integrating the localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure gives the marginalized parameter distribution. In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model, we compare global and localized inference under uniform and skewed context distributions. Localization reduces the reported aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior. An application to the k-$ε$ turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, shows that localized posterior calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration. Both twin experiments are constructed to admit local compensation.

Computation and Language.title: Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness
