Computation and Language.summary: Attention retrieves content precisely, but its scores depend only on query--key products, leaving order and recency to positional encodings. Conversely, state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba-3 track order and recency through input-dependent state transitions that decay and rotate, yet compressing context into a fixed-size state hampers precise retrieval. Hybrids like Samba and Hymba exploit this complementarity only across layers or heads, so SSM transitions never shape attention scores directly. The closest prior work, the Forgetting Transformer (FoX), adds an input-dependent forget gate to the scores but reweights attention by recency alone. We propose SSM-Informed Softmax Attention (SISA), which builds Mamba-3-style state transitions, rotation included, directly into the scores alongside FoX's gate. Each logit receives the weight such an SSM would give that token pair: a decayed match between rotated SSM projections. This rotation already encodes relative position, so SISA drops RoPE; restoring it raises loss. SISA outperforms parameter-matched Transformer and FoX in language modeling and length extrapolation. Among the attention models we compare, hybrids included, only SISA benefits from context beyond the training window. Building SSM transitions into the scores yields stronger attention, and our kernels make it faster and leaner than baselines on their official or standard kernels.

Computation and Language.title: Calculation and rejection diverge in language models tested at known mechanical limits
Computation and Language.summary: When a language model returns engineering quantities with the status "solved", software that trusts it passes them on, even when the requested design is physically impossible. Such failures could reflect poor calculation, how the answer is requested, or a failure to judge feasibility. We set beam loads and disk speeds at known percentages above or below plastic collapse or burst, measured each model's limit calculation separately and tested 12 models in 4,860 calls, including follow-up experiments on new designs. We find that a model can recognize an impossible design when asked only whether it is feasible, yet accept the same design, reporting "solved", when asked for a full answer. Three models accepted beams 10 to 30% beyond collapse despite precise limit calculations in separate questions, and many accepted replies stated the violation. Asked only about feasibility, Opus 5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash rejected every impossible new design they were given, including those accepted in full answers, without false alarms. Rewording when to decline or changing the answer format raised rejection on the original beams, but not consistently on new designs. Software and benchmarks using a model's status should test feasibility judgment and full-answer rejection separately, and report the exact prompt.
Computation and Language.comment: 94 pages, including Supplementary Information. Data and code: https://github.com/nbbllxx0/Certified-feasibility-margins

Computation and Language.title: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
Computation and Language.summary: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

Computation and Language.title: Budget-Aware Compression Pipeline for Single-GPU LLM Inference: Methods, Trade-offs, and Coupling Effects
Computation and Language.summary: Single-GPU deployment of 70B-parameter language models on an NVIDIA GPU is constrained by device memory, long-context throughput, and engineering integration cost. We cast single-GPU inference as a budget-aware design problem over these three axes and study how pruning, quantization, and KV-cache compression interact under realistic execution. Controlled ablations show that layer-wise pruning makes weight quantization more robust. KV-cache sparsification complements INT8 KV quantization by reducing memory without hurting decoding speed, while static vector quantizers often conflict with dynamic caching. Guided by these coupling results and explicit budget tracking, we assembled a practical pipeline and compressed a 70B model to about 33 GB, sustained about 57 tokens/s on 10k token prompts on a single A40, and kept absolute accuracy within 5% on common and reasoning benchmarks. We contribute design rules and a reproducible evaluation protocol that jointly report quality, memory, and end-to-end speed, and we provide a foundation for automated pipeline search under realistic single-GPU constraints.

Statistics Theory.title: Learning Survival Models with Right-Censored Reporting Delays
Statistics Theory.summary: Survival analysis provides statistical methods to model the time until an event occurs. Reporting delays arise when event times are not observed at their occurrence but are only revealed upon reporting. This issue is particularly critical for timely risk evaluation when the observation window is short due to administrative censoring. In this study, we incorporate right-censored reporting delays by jointly modeling parametric hazards for the event and reporting processes. We then construct a consistent estimator for the model parameters and develop a Monte Carlo expectation-maximization algorithm to compute it. To address the challenges posed by administrative censoring, we leverage these findings and propose a transfer-learning procedure. Experimental results demonstrate that our method improves the accuracy of timely risk evaluation under administrative censoring.

Statistics Theory.title: A Spectral Boundary for Independence Learnability
Statistics Theory.summary: Learning independence is fundamental to statistical inference and machine learning, yet learning independence between entire time series by a test remains challenging when only a single observation record is available. Existing guarantees often rely on structural or mixing assumptions, while stationarity and ergodicity alone do not permit consistent testing. In this work, we identify a class-level boundary governed by shared nontrivial Koopman eigenvalues, which represent common persistent oscillatory frequencies of the two processes. When no such eigenvalues are shared, we extend shift-based rank calibration with finite-window dependence witnesses and a data-adaptive threshold to construct a deterministic, weakly consistent test with finite-sample false-positive control, without quantitative mixing assumptions. Conversely, we show that no possibly randomized test can achieve vanishing false-positive probabilities under every independent jointly totally ergodic law while consistently detecting every dependent jointly totally ergodic law with a shared nontrivial eigenvalue. This impossibility already holds for binary observations and persists within any prescribed nonempty open eigenvalue window, identifying a spectral obstruction to universal learning of full-process independence.

Statistics Theory.title: Noise Calibration and Exact Recovery for Multiview Ordinal Rearrangement Data
Statistics Theory.summary: We studied simultaneous recovery of a latent group count, subject partition, and signature means from multiview ordinal ranks. A normalized reference rearrangement score is an affine Spearman correlation; the problem concerns the information retained by several such scores and their noise geometry. We develop an ordered-gap estimator with direction-specific concentration radii. Its finite-sample guarantee separates signature noise, missing groups, and candidate coverage, and allows the group count to grow under an attainable-margin condition. A coordinatewise partition followed by label-tuple refinement recovers groups even when every individual coordinate has population collisions. A binary-code construction explains why the one-dimensional inverse-group margin restriction need not govern a retained coordinate bank. We derive actual-law concentration from bounded ranking modules and a fixed-dimensional combinatorial central limit theorem under an observed permutation representation. A binary ordinal submodel gives logarithmic exact-recovery information scales. A subject-effect construction distinguishes persistent overlap from reducible measurement noise, and an additional ordinal anchor quantifies how new information lowers that error floor. Five focused simulation scenarios illustrate direction-specific calibration, growing-group recovery, coordinate collision resolution, variance reduction, and the effect of an additional ordinal anchor.

Statistics Theory.title: Orthogonal Inference for Conditional Z-Estimation without Cross-Fitting: A Distributional Nearest-Neighbor Approach
Statistics Theory.summary: Estimating conditional parameters, such as heterogeneous treatment effects, often requires rich covariate adjustment, even when the parameters are reported along only a few dimensions. Fitting nuisance functions on the full sample makes all observations available for adjustment, but creates dependence between fitted scores and the observations at which they are evaluated, which is typically avoided by cross-fitting. We develop pointwise inference with full-sample nuisance predictions for exactly identified conditional moment equations, recovering conditional average treatment effects as a special case. We localize the estimating equations around the reporting point using distributional nearest neighbors (DNN), a U-statistic-based averaging procedure. Under sufficient conditions on the local design, orthogonality, prediction accuracy and quantitative deletion stability, the estimator is asymptotically normal, and a frozen-score jackknife consistently estimates its limiting covariance with nuisance predictions held fixed. In simulations, full-sample and cross-fitted inference perform similarly, with coverage shortfalls from nuisance approximation error, spatial bias and heavy studentized tails. An application to 401(k) eligibility using Survey of Income and Program Participation data finds similar estimates across nuisance prediction methods, with wide normal-reference intervals.
Statistics Theory.comment: 36 pages (including appendices and references), 4 figures, 5 tables; supplementary material: 12 pages, 2 figures, 17 tables

Statistics Theory.title: Memorization Capacity of Invariant Convolutional Neural Nets
Statistics Theory.summary: Neural networks are powerful memorizers which are often able to interpolate their training data even when the labels have been randomized. While there exists an extensive literature on the memorization capacity of fully connected networks, in practice more specific architectures with problem-dependent properties are preferred, such as convolutional networks for image classification. In this paper we consider convolutional networks which are invariant with respect to a given arbitrary finite group of orthogonal transformations, which may include translations, reflections, and/or rotations of images and invariances of higher order tensors. We prove upper bounds on the size of an invariant convolutional neural network with threshold activations that is required to interpolate a given dataset with two classes. Our bounds are formulated in terms of a complexity measure that takes the invariant structure into account and is instance-specific, i.e., it is related to the mutual arrangement of the classes in the given dataset and their geometric properties rather than the number of samples. Our proof is constructive: for given input data, instances of an interpolating network can be computed via a randomized algorithm with high probability. In numerical experiments we investigate the practical effectiveness of this algorithm.

Statistics Theory.title: Proximal R2 Priors for Structured Variance Allocation
Statistics Theory.summary: Scientific domain knowledge in regression often concerns structural relationships among model terms, which are typically encoded as parameter constraints. Since such relationships rarely hold exactly in practice, prior distributions should encourage them while at the same time retaining support for scientifically plausible departures. Accounting for these relationships becomes more pressing in modern regression, where high-dimensionality is usually present and regularisation is essential. $R^2$ decomposition priors provide an interpretable foundation for regularisation by placing a prior on total explained variance and distributing the implied signal across model terms. We introduce the Proximal R2 prior, which uses proximal relaxations to encode these relationships as soft constraints on the variance allocation. Our formulation yields differentiable posteriors compatible with standard gradient based samplers. Theoretically, we prove that our prior preserves the characteristic marginal properties of global-local shrinkage priors. Moreover, we establish posterior consistency and contraction rates in growing dimensions, showing that the inclusion of structural relationships and proximal methods do not alter the shrinkage properties. Notably, these results demonstrate that the structural constraints in the model do not hinder posterior recovery. Simulation studies and real-data applications to interaction and generalised additive models demonstrate that our prior improves parameter recovery, out-of-sample prediction, and sampling efficiency over existing constrained and unconstrained shrinkage priors, even under structural misspecification.

Statistics Theory.title: Principal-agent hypothesis testing under adaptive experimentation
Statistics Theory.summary: Principal-agent hypothesis testing studies statistical contracts in which a principal rewards an agent according to data the agent generates. Existing work focuses on the single-shot setting, where the agent produces a single dataset. We extend the framework to sequential settings, where evidence accumulates over time, rewards may be deferred to the end or disbursed incrementally, and the agent may stop the contract at a strategically chosen stopping time. We call a contract null-deterring if no ''null agent'' (those whose data-generating distribution lies in the null hypothesis) can profit in expectation under any stopping rule, and our main conceptual result shows that such contracts are characterized by e-processes. We then turn to the agent's best response and identify the optimal stopping rule through the Snell envelope of the reward process. We develop simpler, more interpretable approximations that often require the agent to have only partial knowledge of its distribution.

Statistics Theory.title: Order invariance of the generalized Rosenblatt transform on standard Borel spaces
Statistics Theory.summary: The Rosenblatt transform maps a random vector to independent uniform variables through successive conditional distribution functions; for laws on $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with atomless conditional distributions and a fixed order of the coordinates, it is the almost surely unique monotone triangular map with this property. For a fixed reference law, transform-based tests remain valid under every fixed admissible order, but that choice can still affect their statistical power. We extend the generalized Rosenblatt transform to laws on countable products of standard Borel spaces, which requires, in addition to an order on the index set, a total order on each component space. For fixed orders, we establish identification and uniqueness results for this extended generalized Rosenblatt transform (EGRT) that parallel those for the classical transform. We then characterize order dependence in two senses: first demonstrating conditions under which the EGRT is invariant under linear extensions of prescribed partial orders, and second showing that under every admissible order the output of the EGRT retains all the statistical information from the input observations over reference-dominated families. We close with a brief discussion of what these results mean for the relationship between order choice and goodness-of-fit testing.

Statistics Theory.title: Central limit theorems for high-dimensional ridge regression under uniform subsampling
Statistics Theory.summary: We study ridge regression based on uniformly subsampled observations in high-dimensional linear models, where the number of predictors and the sample size grow proportionally. Subsampling is implemented through independent Bernoulli indicators with a common selection probability. We establish central limit theorems for linear contrasts of the ridge estimator, allowing for non-Gaussian predictors and general population covariance matrices. Under a vanishing-signal assumption, we obtain an explicit bias correction in the isotropic case and develop consistent estimators of the asymptotic variances. These results enable asymptotically valid tests for linear contrasts of the regression parameter in the isotropic setting. Our proofs exploit the resolvent representation of the ridge estimator and combine leave-one-out arguments with deterministic equivalents from random matrix theory.

Statistics Theory.title: The exact region determined by Blomqvist's beta, Spearman's footrule and Kendall's tau
Statistics Theory.summary: We determine the exact region $Ω_{β,φ,τ}= \{(β(C),φ(C),τ(C))\mid C\in\mathcal{C}\}$ of possible joint values of Blomqvist's beta, Spearman's footrule and Kendall's tau over the class $\mathcal{C}$ of all bivariate copulas. The region consists precisely of all triples $(β,φ,τ)$ satisfying $-1\le β\le 1$, $\frac{3}{16}(1+β)^2-\frac12\le φ\le 1-\frac38(1-β)^2$ and $\frac43 φ-\frac13\le τ\le \frac23 φ+\frac13$. In other words, the known exact $(β,φ)$- and $(φ,τ)$-regions already characterize the joint region, so that, once the value of Spearman's footrule is fixed, Blomqvist's beta imposes no additional restriction on the possible values of Kendall's tau. The proof is constructive: two $2$-parameter families of shuffles of $M$ realize all the points in $Ω_{β,φ,τ}$ with $φ= \frac{3}{16}(1+β)^2-\frac12$, and ordinal sums spread realizations of these two families over the whole region $Ω_{β,φ,τ}$.
Statistics Theory.comment: 15 pages, 6 figures. v2: joint version with L. Ferbar Tratar, D. Kokol Bukovšek, B. Mojškerc and N. Stopar; title and abstract revised

Statistics Theory.title: Optimal Experimental Design for the Polynomial Maximization Method: a Higher-Order Reserve Beyond Second-Order Design Theory
Statistics Theory.summary: Optimal designs for regression with asymmetric errors build on the second-order least squares estimator (SLSE) of Wang and Leblanc (2008), whose gain over ordinary least squares (OLS) comes from the error skewness. With i.i.d. errors the optimally weighted SLSE solves the same estimating equation as the degree-two Polynomial Maximization Method (PMM), a family whose degree-$S$ location estimator has asymptotic variance $g_S\le1$ times that of the sample mean. We derive optimal designs for this family when the errors are independent with constant variance but have standardised cumulants of order three and higher that vary with the regressor (cumulant heteroscedasticity). For a known reduction field $g_S(x)$, the $g_S$-weighted information matrix $M_{g_S}$ obeys the Kiefer-Wolfowitz equivalence theorem. A constant field leaves the OLS-optimal design unchanged; a non-constant field can change it but need not. For symmetric errors with varying kurtosis, the PMM$_2$ and conditional-SLSE designs cannot depart from the OLS-optimal one, whereas a degree-three design can. A stratify-and-pool PMM$_S$ estimator attains $N\mathrm{Cov}(\hatθ)\toσ^2M_{g_S}^{-1}$ at every degree as all strata grow; its per-stratum reduction is below one only for symmetric errors with the symmetry imposed. For a quadratic model on $[0,1]$ with symmetric Beta errors of unit variance and dose-varying shape, the third-order design for the known field has $A$-efficiency $1.047$ relative to the OLS-optimal design, and $1.001$ under the $D$-criterion. A two-stage procedure that estimates the field from a one-third pilot builds designs of $A$-efficiency $1.014$-$1.020$ at $N=600$-$2400$; its realised mean-squared-error ratio against the OLS-optimal design ranges from $0.89$ (a loss) to $1.08$.
Statistics Theory.comment: 41 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Companion to arXiv:2606.11421 (second-order least squares as the degree-two polynomial maximization method). v3: adds the cost of a small asymmetry and the limit of plug-in designs; corrects the two-stage limit; code supplement v1.0.2

Statistics Theory.title: Optimal In-context Adaptivity and Distributional Robustness of Transformers
Statistics Theory.summary: We study in-context learning problems where a Transformer is pretrained on tasks drawn from a mixture distribution $π=\sum_{α\in\mathcal{A}} λ_α π_α$, called the pretraining prior, in which each mixture component $π_α$ is a distribution on tasks of a specific difficulty level indexed by $α$. Our goal is to understand the performance of the pretrained Transformer when evaluated on a different test distribution $μ$, consisting of tasks of fixed difficulty $β\in\mathcal{A}$, and with potential distribution shift relative to $π_β$, subject to the chi-squared divergence $χ^2(μ,π_β)$ being at most $κ$. In particular, we consider nonparametric regression problems with random smoothness, and multi-index models with both random smoothness and random effective dimension. We prove that a large Transformer pretrained on sufficient data achieves the optimal rate of convergence corresponding to the difficulty level $β$, uniformly over test distributions $μ$ in the chi-squared divergence ball. Thus, the pretrained Transformer is able to achieve faster rates of convergence on easier tasks and is robust to distribution shift at test time. Finally, we prove that even if an estimator had access to the test distribution $μ$, the convergence rate of its expected risk over $μ$ could not be faster than that of our pretrained Transformers, thereby providing a more appropriate optimality guarantee than minimax lower bounds.

Statistics Theory.title: Diagnosing parameter unidentifiability in stochastic dynamics with an application to flocking models
Statistics Theory.summary: Although flocking behaviour has been studied extensively in active matter physics and mathematical biology, methods for assessing parameter estimability remain underdeveloped. For models formulated as stochastic differential equations (SDEs), we develop a Hessian-based diagnostic framework that detects unidentifiable directions and indicates whether, and how, estimation precision can be improved. The framework utilizes the submartingale structure of the loss function's Hessian and tracks its minimum eigenvalue over time. Under convergence of the time-averaged Hessian, we prove that this eigenvalue grows linearly for identifiable models, but only sublinearly, as $o(t)$, for unidentifiable ones; for a specific type of parameter redundancy, this $o(t)$ bound is tightened to $o(\sqrt{t}\log t)$. Applying the framework to stochastic flocking models, we demonstrate that, in identifiable settings, the magnitude of the eigenvalue reflects the attainable estimation precision. We further uncover a physical mechanism of unidentifiability: as the system approaches the ordered state, the parameters become algebraically degenerate, even though the model contains no trivial redundancy. Identifiability therefore depends on the dynamical regime, not only on model structure. Our framework offers a practical tool for reliable parameter estimation, not only in flocking models but in SDE models across diverse fields.
Statistics Theory.comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, Supplementary Information available as an ancillary file

Statistics Theory.title: High-dimensional two-sample testing: From optimal transport to optimal derangements
Statistics Theory.summary: In recent years, optimal transport has emerged as a useful framework for constructing distribution-free multivariate two-sample tests by transporting observations to a reference distribution under a suitable transportation cost. However, existing optimal transport-based tests can perform poorly in high dimension, low sample size (HDLSS) settings, and their performance depends critically on the choice of the reference distribution and transportation cost. We investigate this phenomenon and show that suitable choices can substantially improve their performance. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a class of two-sample tests based on optimal derangements that do not require an external reference distribution. The minimum distance pairing test of Rosenbaum arises as a special case when the optimization is restricted to a subclass of derangements, thereby revealing a connection between this method and optimal transport. We propose the optimal derangement (ODER) test and its distribution-free variant, the ODER-SHC test, obtained by restricting the minimization to derangements consisting of a single Hamiltonian cycle. We establish their consistency under both HDLSS and classical large-sample asymptotic regimes. We also develop corresponding procedures based on the $L1$ distance and establish their high-dimensional consistency under conditions involving coordinate-wise energy distances. These $L1$ distance based tests can also discriminate between two high-dimensional distributions with identical first two moments but different marginal distributions. Analyses of benchmark datasets and extensive simulation studies demonstrate the performance of the proposed methods across a variety of alternatives and data settings.

Statistics Theory.title: Poincaré's Inequality on Sliding-Window Occupation Count Kernels and the Optimal Normalized Spectral-Gap Constant
Statistics Theory.summary:
Let $P$ be an irreducible reversible Markov kernel on an $m$-state space $Ω$, and denote its right spectral gap by $\Gap(P) =1-λ_2(P)$. For a stationary trajectory, let $K_t$ be the occupation-count vector of the length-$n$ window beginning at time $t$. The stationary pair $(K_0,K_1)$ defines a reversible projected count kernel $\widetilde P_n$. For each fixed $m\ge2$, define \[
  c_m^\star=
  \inf_{\substack{|Ω|=m,\ P\ \mathrm{irreducible\ and\ reversible}
  n\ge2}}
  \frac{n\Gap(\widetilde P_n)}{\Gap(P)}. \] We prove \[
  \frac1{1080m}\le c_m^\star\le q_{m-2},
  \qquad
  q_0=\frac14,\quad q_{r+1}=q_r(1-q_r). \] We also show $q_{m-2}=(m+\log m+O(1))^{-1}$, which implies that $c_m^\star=Θ(m^{-1})$. Thus, the reciprocal optimal comparison coefficient $C_m^{\mathrm{opt}}=(c_m^\star)^{-1}$ is of the order $m$. In the two-state case, we determine the exact values $c_2^\star=1/4$ and $C_2^{\mathrm{opt}}=4$. %the exact constants for $m\ge3$ remain open. The lower bound also holds for $n=1$ and is uniform in $P$, including sparse and periodic kernels. The proof combines short-window decorrelation with an averaged anchor-excursion decomposition, a Green-kernel hitting estimate, and a stopped Carleson--Hardy inequality. A nested rare-state construction produces finite $m$-state witnesses whose normalized Rayleigh quotients approach $q_{m-2}$ through an ordered sequence of limits. For every fixed finite irreducible reversible aperiodic kernel on at least two states, $\Gap(\widetilde P_n)=Θ_P(n^{-1})$.

Statistics Theory.title: Maximizing R{é}nyi Entropy over the Transportation Polytope: Structure and Algorithm
Statistics Theory.summary: We study the problem of finding the minimum $\mathbb{L}\_2$-norm element in a transportation polytope. It corresponds to minimizing the index of coincidence or maximizing R{é}nyi entropy over joint probability distributions with prescribed marginals. The solution is straightforward under a feasibility condition on the marginals. We make three contributions. First, we decompose the basic solution into a mixture of three interpretable couplings and derive a closed-form sampling procedure, revealing its role as the $\mathbb{L}\_2$-projection of the uniform distribution onto the transportation polytope. Second, we show that the feasibility condition becomes exponentially rare as the number of modalities grows, which highlights the practical necessity of a more general construction. Third, we provide a KKT-based iterative construction of the optimal coupling for arbitrary marginals with explicit Lagrange multipliers.

Statistics Theory.title: The Bernstein-von Mises theorem and efficiency for semiparametric inference in multivariate Hawkes processes
Statistics Theory.summary: In this paper, we study semiparametric inference for linear multivariate Hawkes processes, a class of point processes widely used to describe self and mutually exciting phenomena. We establish a convolution theorem giving the best limiting distribution for a regular estimator of smooth functional. Then, in the Bayesian setting, we prove a semiparametric Bernstein-von Mises (BvM) theorem for nonparametric random series priors. We apply this result to histogram and wavelet based priors. Taken together, the convolution and BvM theorems show that, from a frequentist point of view, semiparametric Bayesian procedures have asymptotically the optimal behavior. Deriving the BvM property for random series priors led us to prove L2 posterior contraction, complementing for these priors the results of Donnet, Rivoirard and Rousseau (2020).

Statistics Theory.title: On the Role of Normalization in Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding for 1-bit Compressed Sensing
Statistics Theory.summary: Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding (BIHT) is a simple, yet effective, greedy method for recovering a sparse vector from one-bit sign measurements. In its original form, BIHT performs a ``gradient-descent'' step, followed by hard thresholding. A convergence analysis of this algorithm was left open in the introductory work of Jacques, Laska, Boufounos, and Baraniuk [IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory (2013)] and has remained unresolved for over a decade, with subsequent sharp analyses studying a normalized variant instead, that additionally projects every iterate onto the unit sphere. This paper resolves that gap and characterizes when per-iterate normalization is algorithmically necessary. In the noiseless setting, we prove a universal, sample-optimal convergence theorem for the original BIHT algorithm. Specifically, with $\widetilde O(s/ε)$ measurements, a deterministic, computable finite-time iterate has directional error at most $ε$, simultaneously for every $s$-sparse unit vector. This matches the optimal sample dependence achieved by normalized BIHT in prior work. Under sign corruptions, we prove a sharp separation. If at most a $τ$ fraction of signs are flipped adversarially, then BIHT, without per-iterate normalization, still reaches the robust error floor at an early iterate with a matching $\widetilde O(s/ε)$ sample complexity rate as its normalized variant. This recovery, however, is not stable. We prove a scalar lower bound showing that any nontrivial corruption pattern, even one that involves only one flipped sign together with one clean sign, forces the iterates to oscillate indefinitely. Consequently, no general last-iterate convergence theorem can hold for BIHT under sign corruptions, while its normalized surrogate provably escapes this instance.

Statistics Theory.title: Regression Functions as Fields on Covariate Space: Evolution Equations, the Hessian, and Identification
Statistics Theory.summary: For each time $t$, the regression function $m_t(x)=E[Y_t\mid X_t=x]$ of an outcome on contemporaneous covariates can be regarded as a field on covariate space. When the covariates of units move as a diffusion and each unit's outcome has its own dynamics, we show that $m_t$ satisfies a second-order evolution equation whose diffusion term is $\frac12\mathrm{tr}(Σ\nabla^2 m_t)$, the Hessian of the regression function weighted by the covariance $Σ$ of covariate increments, whose transport term is the drift of the time-reversed covariate process, and whose source term is the conditional mean rate of change of the outcome; this yields a Feynman-Kac representation along reversed covariate paths. We relate this Hessian to quadratic regression (under Gaussian design the best quadratic approximation has Hessian $E[\nabla^2 m(X)]$) and to kernel smoothing bias. For bistable replicator dynamics on covariate space, travelling fronts are exactly logistic in $(x,t)$, so one logistic regression identifies the diffusion-reaction ratio and the invading strategy. We then ask whether spread in covariate space reflects fluctuating unit characteristics or imitation among similar units. Imitation acts through exactly the same operator as covariate fluctuation, so the two are observationally equivalent in the regression field; panel data separate them because they identify $Σ$ directly. The two cannot be separated on a travelling front, and we propose a split-sample instrumental-variables test that works on seeded, non-front profiles, with size and power evaluated in agent-based experiments.
Statistics Theory.comment: 13 pages, 2 figures. Code for the symbolic checks and simulations is included as ancillary files

Statistics Theory.title: Scalable Bayesian Quadrature via Operator-Adapted Features
Statistics Theory.summary: Kernel methods face two recurrent bottlenecks: the cubic cost of inverting an $n\times n$ kernel matrix, as in kernel ridge regression, and the evaluation of kernel integrals, as required in kernel quadrature. Existing low-rank kernel and Gaussian process approximations primarily address the former bottleneck, but do not control the downstream quadrature error when both the kernel matrix and kernel mean are approximated, particularly when the integrand lies outside the kernel reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We address both challenges through an operator-adapted finite-feature approximation. Specifically, we construct a finite-dimensional working kernel from the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of a second-order differential operator. We establish convergence guarantees for the resulting finite-feature estimators in kernel quadrature, with extension to other related kernel methods. Our results show that, with $m \lesssim n$ basis functions, the truncated estimator attains the corresponding benchmark statistical rates. The theory covers fixed/random designs, noisy/noiseless observations, oversmoothing/undersmoothing regimes, and Matérn/Gaussian-type weights. We provide explicit error bounds that quantify the roles of the spectral cutoff, regularization parameter, lengthscale, sampling geometry, and operator boundary condition. We verify the convergence results in numerical experiments.

Statistics Theory.title: Averaged Annealed Markov Chains Achieve the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA, Part II: Langevin Dynamics
Statistics Theory.summary: We consider the tensor principal components analysis (tensor PCA) problem on the sphere, in which we are asked to recover an unknown vector in $\mathcal{S}_N=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N:\lVert x\rVert^2=N\}$ from a noisy observation of its $k$-th tensor power, for a fixed $k\ge3$. Tensor PCA exhibits a well-studied information-computation gap: global algorithms such as spectral methods and sum-of-squares work above an algorithmic threshold, below which we know matching lower bounds (against these and some other restricted models of computation). In contrast, local algorithms such as Markov chains were only known to succeed from a random initialization at a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio, and were believed to be inferior to global algorithms for tensor PCA. Continuing the program initiated in Part I [arXiv:2610.16705], we show that spherical Langevin dynamics, when supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization. Together with Part I, our results demonstrate that local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start.
Statistics Theory.comment: Companion paper to arXiv:2610.16705 (Part I). 71 pages, 1 figure

Statistics Theory.title: Strong approximations for dependent random fields
Statistics Theory.summary: We establish strong Gaussian approximations for centered stationary random fields on $\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge2$, represented as measurable functions of i.i.d.\ innovations. Under finite $p$th moments, $p>2$, and sufficiently fast decay of spatial dependence, we construct a single coupling of the field with an i.i.d.\ Gaussian field. Its partial sums, scaled by the long-run standard deviation, approximate those of the original field almost surely, uniformly over all rectangular prefixes and all observation scales. Over a cube of side length $n$, the approximation error is $O_{\mathrm{a.s.}}(n^{\max\{d/p,(d-1)/2\}})$ up to logarithmic factors. While $d/p$ is the familiar moment term, the surface term $(d-1)/2$, absent for independent planar arrays, emerges as a cost of dependence, and cannot be removed even for finite-range Gaussian fields. The assumptions accommodate nonlinear and noncausal fields without imposing mixing. The proof combines a permanent dyadic blocking, a local Gaussian coupling in tensor Haar coordinates driven by a Doob martingale with vanishing conditional third moments, and a comparison of the resulting dependent Gaussian blocks with white noise.

Statistics Theory.title: On the Spherical Dirichlet Distribution: Corrections and Results
Statistics Theory.summary: This article revisits the spherical-Dirichlet distribution (SDD) introduced by Guardiola (2020) and clarifies the correction to its density presented in an earlier version of this preprint. The principal issue concerns Equation (3) of the original publication, which expresses the density in local Euclidean coordinates rather than with respect to spherical surface-area measure. We derive the corrected intrinsic density and revisit its moments, covariance matrix, mode, and limiting properties. We show that the two density representations describe the same probability distribution, preserving the moment formulas and likelihood-based parameter estimation. However, the mode and uniformity conditions depend on the reference measure and require corresponding clarification. Reported simulation and text mining estimates are revisited and updated. The resulting presentation reconciles the original construction with its intrinsic spherical properties.
Statistics Theory.comment: 9 pages, 1 figure with four panels. Revised to clarify coordinate and spherical surface-area densities, mode and uniformity conditions, and parameter estimation; numerical summaries updated. Corrects and extends Guardiola, J. Stat. Distrib. App. 7, 6 (2020), https://doi.org/10.1186/s40488-020-00106-9
